subsubtopic: FOREST FIRE FIGHTING CAPABILITY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again forest fires are raging out of control in northern British Columbia, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories, destroying vast areas of virgin forest land, the life and habitat of all species of wildlife, and causing extensive damage to property and serious threat to human life. This kind of natural calamity of course cannot be contained within political boundaries of territories and provinces, and it is for reasons of conflicting and overlapping jurisdiction and responsibility that the present situation in the north has once again reached such monumental proportions. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) and any other hon. member who wants to associate himself with this motion:
That this House urges the government to establish and maintain through the Ministry of National Defence, and in co-ordination with the provinces, the capability to respond quickly with equipment and manpower to forest fires anywhere in Canada and, further, to establish within the Canadian forest service a much improved program and capacity in the area of forest fire prevention.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Revenue, of which I have given him notice. When filing their tax returns, 50 people across the country made out cheques to the Peace Tax Fund representing 10.5 per cent of their income tax, which is the percentage that goes to the Department of National Defence. As conscientious objectors, they did not wish their tax money to be spent on weapons or the armed forces. Eight of these cheques were accepted by the department and were cleared by their banks or credit unions. Therefore, the minister is now holding a significant amount of money in the Peace Tax Fund. Since this money has been accepted and deposited, what is the minister planning to do with this Peace Tax money?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FILING OF INCOME TAX RETURNS BY CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. I am not aware that any funds so earmarked have been banked. Indeed, I know of one case where the cheque was sent back which had been addressed to the Department of National Defence because the Income Tax Act does not permit the targeting of tax dollars to any specific project, policy or fund. People may have views and may hold them very sincerely, but the withholding of income tax for special purposes is not a legitimate form of protest.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the answer, but it seems that the group which has been managing this kind of protest has recorded that, of the 40 cheques which have been handled by the department, there are at least five policies. First, the cheque is cashed and the taxpayer told he owes no more money. Second, the taxpayer is told that the cheque has to be made out to the Receiver General and that he still owes the money. Third, he is told that he has to pay the money with interest. Fourth, he is told that he has to pay the money with interest, plus a fine. Why is there so much uncertainty within the department if the policy is quite clear as to how to handle these kinds of things? They seem to have at least five different policies. How can the minister justify that?

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF NAVAL RESERVE HEADQUARTERS FROM HALIFAX TO QUEBEC CITY-CABINET POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question concerning Canada's naval reserve force which I would like to address to the Prime Minister because it really does involve important government policy.
The Prime Minister now knows that a decision has been made to transfer naval reserve headquarters from Halifax to Quebec City. What he may not know is that this decision has shocked both civilian and military officials because it does not relate to national defence. I want to ask the Prime Minister this: was the decision approved by the cabinet, does the cabinet endorse the decision and, if it was not so approved, will the Prime Minister immediately order a review of the decision by a committee of cabinet or a committee of Parliament? If the decision is sensibly reviewed, I know it will be reversed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF NAVAL RESERVE HEADQUARTERS FROM HALIFAX TO QUEBEC CITY-CABINET POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would be happy if any minister wanted to raise this in full cabinet. We have a full cabinet meeting on Thursday and, if any minister wants to raise it, I would be happy to deal with it.
The reason why this decision was taken by the minister, on the advice of his officials and of military people themselves, is pretty straightforward. There is not a high enough percentage of Francophones in the navy, and we think it is important that some naval operations be conducted out of Quebec City. That is a simple fact established by statistics. Whereas in the armed forces in general some 26 per cent of the forces are Francophone, in the case of the navy I believe the average is around 13 per cent for other ranks and as low as 10 per cent or 11 per cent for officers.
I think this is an important and progressive move. It will not prevent the naval forces remaining in Halifax from growing. It will simply ensure that some of the services of the navy will be delivered out of Quebec City.

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF NAVAL RESERVE HEADQUARTERS FROM HALIFAX TO QUEBEC CITY-CABINET POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the real concern is that this is only the first in a series of initiatives designed to give the naval force a greater presence in the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my supplementary question to the Secretary of State, particularly in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has suggested a cabinet review.
The Secretary of State now knows that the reason for this move of naval reserve headquarters from Halifax to Quebec City is to increase Francophone participation in the naval
reserve and in Canada's navy. As the person responsible for the administration of the Official Languages Act I would like to ask him whether he thinks this is a fair extension of the provisions of that act and whether he thinks it is a proper exercise of power and authority under that act and within the intent of that act. Does he think that the interests of this nation in terms of national defence should govern over considerations like Francophone participation in the navy and the extent to which there is a certain number of Francophones versus a certain number of Anglophones? What does that have to do with guns, bullets, and national defence?

Lippincott of Canada to close. The company will be closed as a result of a FIRA decision because there is no Canadian buyer. If I may quote the most likely Canadian buyer, they said that "it would be more profitable" for Lippincott to close the Canadian operation and export books from the United States to Canada rather than selling to a Canadian. Given that description of Lippincott's problem by its most likely buyer, why does the minister continue to adhere to such a vicious double standard? In the Maislin case, American jobs are guaranteed with Canadian money, while in the Lippincott case, where 100 per cent of the


jobs are Canadian, the minister remains firmly and pigheadedly committed to putting 12 Canadians out of work and forcing those jobs into the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: DECISION AFFECTING LIPPINCOTT COMPANY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the government is not forcing Lippincott to close. That is a decision of the foreign parent, which we deplore, and which it is not being forced to take by this government. It has a number of alternatives available, including making a new application to the government, including seeking a Canadian for a joint venture, and including selling to Canadians. The Association of Canadian Book Publishers has said that it knows of three Canadian firms willing to buy that company. So, Madam Speaker, we are not forcing the company to close. It is a decision of the foreign parent. It is the foreign parent that is putting Canadians out of work. With respect to Maislin, we are saving 2,000 Canadian jobs. There is no double standard; we are being consistent.

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING ACHIEVEMENT OF BENEFIT FOR CANADA
QUERY RESPECTING ACHIEVEMENT OF BENEFIT FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is sometimes difficult to get ministers to listen. May I repeat what the most likely buyer, the president of Gage Publishing, had to say in The Globe and Mail this morning. Presumably the minister only read the headline. He said that "it would be more profitable" for Lippincott to close. The minister is saying that the new foreign investment policy of this country is that if a firm is profitable and can make money, it should get out.
FIRA's job is to decide whether substantial benefits accrue to Canada from foreign investment. Can the minister explain to the House, and to the 12 Canadians who will lose their jobs on November 20, what significant benefit is achieved for them or for Canada when their jobs disappear and there is no food on their tables?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING ACHIEVEMENT OF BENEFIT FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the decision with respect to the Lippincott application was taken in June, 1981, by the cabinet. On the basis of the information presented, it was found that there was not significant benefit in terms of, among other things, consistency with the long-standing policy of the government to encourage a greater Canadian presence in book publishing and book distribution.
The government has not told Lippincott Canada to close. The announcement the company made the other day was not as a result of any order by the government but as a result of a decision taken by the foreign parent. That is a decision it does not have to take at this time, and it is a decision it has taken in spite of the fact that alternatives are open to it. If it does not want to take those alternatives, it has to bear the responsibility-a regrettable one-for the action that my hon. friend is talking about.

subsubtopic: PLACEMENT OF INMATES IN DOUBLE CELLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. Recently he announced a new policy of placement of inmates in a number of federal penitentiaries in double cells. Both staff and prisoners have strongly protested this policy, arguing that it will lead to increased tensions in the institution and possibly even to violence.
In view of the fact that this policy of placement of two prisoners in cells built for one runs completely contrary to the 1977 report of the subcommittee on penitentiaries, and contrary to any sound correctional philosophy, and could lead to serious incidents in the institutions affected, will the minister now agree to end this dangerous policy of double-cell usage in federal institutions? Further, particularly in light of the recent tragic deaths at Archambault, when will the minister finally implement the key recommendations of the 1977 unanimous subcommittee report which he has so far completely ignored?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: PLACEMENT OF INMATES IN DOUBLE CELLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there are no double-cell occupancies in Archambault, so obviously that was not a factor in the tragic incident there. In general, my answer to the hon. member is that inmates are being put two to a cell in a limited number of institutions because we have no other place to put them. We do not have new institutions coming onstream to provide extra capacity for another couple of years. The indications I have from the correctional services are that they anticipate extra inmate population as a temporary problem and that it will decline within the next couple of years. I would like to put to him that at this particular point, with the responsibility we have at law to incarcerate federal offenders, what other option is there to double celling at this time?

subsubtopic: PLACEMENT OF INMATES IN DOUBLE CELLS
speechtext: One of the key recommendations of the 1977 subcommittee report was to look seriously at alternatives to incarceration. If we looked at that, perhaps it would deal with the question of overcrowding.

Madam Speaker, I understand that I have three minutes left in which to conclude my argument with regard to Motion No. 4 which stands in my name. The intent of that motion is to restore collective bargaining rights to employees of the Canadian Pacific railway system and to employees of the other four railways the government has decided to include in the bill, although all five of those railways are in the private sector. We will present a similar motion later on which would also state that Canadian National should be excluded from the provisions of this bill.
It is our belief that the railway system is a very important sector in the Canadian economy. Through good management in negotiation arrangements involving Canadian Pacific, Canadian National, the other companies and the unions, we have managed to have railway peace over the last number of years in this country. Therefore, not only do we find the bill itself to be repugnant, but we also find it very dangerous that the government will break a collective agreement which has already been reached between the railways and their unions. After negotiations have already been settled and after an agreement has been signed by the respective parties, 1 think it is very dangerous to break it.
This will result in many problems for Canadians in the future, not only for the companies and the unions, but also for farmers and communities which rely on those railways. That is because at the end of this wage control period, the members of those unions will want to catch up. For each of the next two years, they will lose 6 per cent and 5 per cent. At the end of that time, they will want to catch up. I and fellow members of my caucus cannot see how we can have railway peace two years hence when all those workers will suddenly attempt to catch up and regain the wages to which they had already agreed but which have been lost strictly because of the government's action.
We therefore argue that the amendment with regard to CP and our later amendment with regard to CN must pass. I would hope that Conservatives and Liberals from all parts of the country who are concerned about the transportation system would support our amendments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to speak in the debate on Bill C-124, particularly because of the comments by hon. members from both opposition parties in the debate yesterday, which I had the opportunity to hear. Each hon. member from the opposition parties told us how the Canadian economy would be radically different if the government followed their prescriptions or if they were in power. They said it would be much improved and we would not be encountering today's unfortunate problems.
These prescriptions reminded me of a recent article in Forbes magazine. The article, an interview of the French historian, Fernand Braudel, was captioned "Inflation; poverty; dying industries: The crisis is universal, a great historian tells Forbes. Politicians who promise quick cures are fools or liars."
I believe that anyone listening to the debate in the last day or two and hearing these prescriptions from the two opposition parties would come to the rather rapid conclusion that we have plenty of fools and liars in the House. An illustration is the state of the auto industry in North America. We are all familiar with the problems it has had in the past several years involving imports and its production of automobiles which are not up to world standard. As a result, there have been tremendous lay-offs throughout the industry. There have been many studies of the problems of that industry. One which I recently had the opportunity to read was carried out for the task force on employment opportunities in the 1980s. This study, entitled "The Medium-Term Employment Outlook in the Canadian Automotive Industry", discussed the state of the industry and tried to predict the number of persons who would be employed in that industry in Canada over the course of the next ten years.
In 1980, the Canadian automotive industry employed approximately 98,000 workers. The study forecast that in 1985, not allowing for offshore procurement, it would employ somewhere in the neighbourhood of 64,000 to 73,000 workers, which would mean a decrease of approximately 34,000 workers, if one wants to take the lower limit. Allowing for offshore procurement, that is, if the automotive industry were to purchase parts from foreign countries, the automotive industry would employ only something in the neighbourhood of 53,000 to 60,000 workers in 1985. By 1990, even a further reduction is predicted. The forecast, again not taking into account offshore procurement, is that approximately 50,000 to 55,000 workers would be employed; or allowing for offshore procurement, only
41,000	to 45,000 would be employed.
You have there, Mr. Speaker, an authoritative study which predicted that even under the best of circumstances the Canadian automobile industry will employ in ten years from 1980, which is eight years from now, approximately half the number of workers it employed in 1980. I quote from the conclusion of this study:
Essentially we are looking at an industry whose size and work force in North America will contract, even if the same number of vehicles are purchased, because of changes in production technology.
1 defy the members of the opposition to tell us how they, if they were in power, would change this employment outlook. The problems which the Canadian economy is facing today are complex. They require all the ingenuity that Canadians can muster in order to solve them. To suggest that interest rates can be magically lowered, as is often proposed by the New Democratic Party, or that all of our problems can be solved by less government intervention, is foolish.
Recently we had an example of how the prescriptions or preconceived notions of the New Democratic Party fit in with reality in the study on bank profits. The two members of the NDP who sat on that committee walked out of the committee hearing when it turned out that the facts did not fit the ideas they had when the hearing started. As my colleague said, their attitude is "don't confuse us with the facts".
We had a similar example of the prescription of the Progressive Conservative Party, that less government intervention will solve all the problems. The best example 1 can cite is Chrysler Corporation. Because of the structural problems I was referring to and because of bad management and a failure to keep up with advanced technology in other countries, it was on the verge of bankruptcy several years ago. Governments in the United States and Canada decided that, given the importance of the automobile industry in North America, the number of people it employed and the subsidiary industries that relied upon the help of that industry, it was necessary to provide certain loan guarantees and government support in order to get that company back on its feet. Assistance was given only when it was assured the company had a plan and ideas to restructure itself and improve its techniques in order to produce more efficient cars which the public would be willing to buy. Naturally those in the Conservative Party abhorred that kind of government intervention. They felt the government should not get involved. Even today when the government sees fit to help other companies experiencing similar difficulties, we hear the same cry-"No, the government should not get involved".
What is the proof of the pudding? Several weeks ago Chrysler Corporation announced the largest last quarter profit in the past four or five years and seems to be well on the road to recovery. That is proof that simplistic solutions from the Conservative Party do not provide the answers to the ills of the Canadian economy.
This bill proposes that increases in wages of public servants be limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over the next two years. As could very well be expected, the plan has been vilified by both of the opposition parties and by members of the press. Jack McArthur, in a column in the Montreal Gazette of July 2, 1982, stated as follows:
It's not possible to have one group of Canadian workers and organizations heading for long toward a chilly austerity not noticeably suffered by the remainder. Over time, that would bring an indigestibly large number of economic distortions, demonstrations, strikes, resentments and political difficulties.
He has criticized our program. It is clear that the circumstances which he cites support our program. Certain parts of


the economy are suffering from the recession and from the transformation that is taking place in our society. They have been asked to bear the burden solely, without help from other segments of the economy.
There are two good reasons for supporting this program and this legislation. The first is on the basis of equity and the second on the basis of competition. As I was mentioning, certain industries are being asked to bear the burden of this recession and the structural changes taking place in Canadian society. Other sectors, such as the public sector, are not subject to market forces. They are removed from competition. The workers do not negotiate under the same constraints as those in areas of the economy that are subject to competition.
In those areas of the economy that are not subject to competition and the kind of technological change which is hurting certain sectors of the economy, it is only logical that those most fortunate people be asked to contribute to the improvement and restructuring of those parts of the economy undergoing such difficulties. In a few moments I will get into some of the efforts the government is making to help with the restructuring of the industries to which 1 was referring.
As I mentioned earlier, the second reason for supporting this legislation is competition. Certain sectors are facing competition from industries overseas and in the United States. I am familiar with a number of companies which bid on contracts in the United States or in other countries. 1 am sure all hon. members are familiar with similar companies in their constituencies or in their areas of the country.
As I mentioned yesterday in the few brief remarks I made, 30 per cent of Canada's gross national product comes from exports, whereas only 10 per cent of the gross national products of the United States and Japan are dependent on exports. This indicates the extent to which Canada has had to trade in order to survive. I am familiar with certain companies which in recent years have had to bid on contracts in the United States. They have had to put up with wage increases which have far exceeded increases in productivity and far exceeded the level of wage increases in the United States.
There is a particular company of which I am aware which has a plant in an area of Montreal and another plant in the state of Vermont. Some time ago I was talking with the president of that company-this was before the recent devaluation of the Canadian dollar-and he told me that he paid his workers in the plant in Vermont approximately $4 per hour less, all things being considered, including the exchange rate, yet the workers in the two plants were doing essentially the same work. Recently this company had to go through wage negotiations again. As we know, settlements in the United States have recently been in the order of 4 per cent or 5 per cent in some industries, but the Canadian workers in this particular company asked for increases of something in the order of 10 per cent. The president of the company said no, he would not go beyond 6 per cent, and he encouraged the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
workers to follow the lead which had been taken by the Government of Canada and to understand the extent to which their jobs were dependent upon showing restraint. I am happy to say they agreed to that. They agreed to increases of 6 per cent, and hopefuly this company will continue to prosper and grow.
What would have been the case if the government had not changed its policy, if we were going along oblivious to the difficulties being experienced by many sectors of the economy and allowed increases in the order of 10 per cent or 11 per cent? It would certainly be a very difficult situation. It would be almost untenable for people in more competitive industries and those open to international competition to go to their workers and ask them to accept something less.
1 think I have demonstrated that this program can be supported both on the basis of equity and for competitive reasons.
1 believe my time is up. I wanted to say a few words about the national training program which has just been adopted by the government. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crom-bie) described it as the most significant piece of legislation we will pass in this session. Unfortunately, 1 did not have a chance to get into that. 1 hope to come back to that at an early opportunity, and I thank hon. members for this opportunity to express my views on this subject.

This part applies to employees of Canadian Pacific Limited and its subsidiaries who are employed in the operation of a railway and to the employees of the following:

speechtext: Let's make them public. Let's nationalize them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
We know Ian Sinclair came to Ottawa to head the private sector in pushing this bill through. In my speech the other day on one of the other clauses 1 questioned the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) about meetings they had with railway representatives. The government has added to this bill the railways 1 have cited with the consent of the Conservative


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
Party, and the result for employees of these railways will be misery. The hon. member for Rosedale said that the New Democratic Party is not acting in a responsible way and that we are in serious trouble. Yes, we are in serious trouble, and one of the reasons is that since 1978, almost $30 billion has been spent on takeovers by large multinational corporations. Half that, a staggering $14 billion, was spent in the first nine months of 1981, but not one job was created by those takeovers.
Ian Sinclair is chairman and chief executive officer of Canadian Pacific Enterprises Limited, and the list of his directorships goes on and on. However, I will name only one. He is a director of the Royal Bank of Canada. It is interesting to note that other corporate elite tied into Canada's corporate structure also sit on the boards of directors of the Bank of Montreal and other major banks across Canada. This corporate elite is neatly tied together to dictate interest rate policy and other policies to the government. The Conservative Party is following suit with the corporate elite right down the line. Members of the Conservative Party want to steal money from workers while these takeovers take place.
Small businessmen are losing their businesses because all this money is tied into big multinational takeovers. The boards of directors of banks have clearly directed bank money into takeovers which have not created one job but have taken money away from small businessmen. A small businessman who walks into a bank wanting to borrow money finds that the money is already taken by the big corporate elite for the purpose of takeovers but not for the purpose of creating one job. I brought this matter up in committee and was told that this was done in the energy field. What energy is involved in the Hudson's Bay Company taking over Zeller's? Where are the extra jobs in such programs?
Another interesting gentleman sits on the board of directors of CP Rail, the Hon. John Turner, a former minister of finance with the Liberal government. Let me list his directorships. He is a partner in McMillan, Binch which is located in the Royal Bank Plaza in Toronto; a director of Canadian Investment Fund, Ltd.; Canadian Pacific Ltd.; Credit Foncier; MacMillan, Bloedel Ltd.; Marathon Realty Co. Ltd.; Massey-Ferguson Ltd.; Sandoz (Canada) Ltd.; The Seageam Co. Ltd.; Wander Ltd. Those are the directorships he holds. We begin to see the tie-in between the Liberal government, the former Conservative government and who they represent.
We heard members of the Conservative Party say how concerned they are about jobs. If they are so concerned and if the government is so concerned, then why do they not tell Ian Sinclair to build his ships in Canada and man them with Canadian merchant marines instead of flying the flag of another country? Those are the kinds of programs that should be put in place in order to put people back to work.
I want to speak about the bill as it affects workers, Mr. Speaker. I feel that members of this House do not understand the problems there are in the railways industry. The President of the Treasury Board has no knowledge of what is going on in
the Department of Labour. He has literally smashed Part III, Part IV and Part V of the Canada Labour Code.
Over the last few years the unions on the railways and in many Crown corporations have been negotiating contracts on actual problems and actual costs. They agreed to build a COLA clause into the last two contracts to provide that the money agreed to would be collected the following year. In other words, if the cost of living went up the year after, then they got an increase; but if it did not, then they received nothing. Of course, the cost of living is going up. The government knows that it will continue going up, so now it is going to freeze the wages of the people concerned.
If that is done, then what happens to the local union representation on the railway system? What happens to the people representing the workers and who have to deal with their problems? When you take away the initiative of having something to bargain for, the initiative to deal with health and safety problems, and you tell the workers these are monetary problems and cannot be dealt with, it is no wonder that people are reluctant to join the union executive.
I want to talk about the slides that come down the mountains, Mr. Speaker. When they shoot the slides down and the trains come down the hill and they wait, a clause in the railway workers' agreement says that after ten or eleven hours of duty they are entitled to go home. But many dedicated employees will wait and continue to carry out their duties. What kind of working relationships will there be when there is this kind of hardship?
When Mr. L. A. Hill, who is manager of Canadian Pacific's western lines at Vancouver, was superintendent of the Revel-stoke division, he wrote a letter commending the workers for their dedication during very, very serious snow conditions. That took place in a spirit of co-operation, not a spirit of confrontration, Mr. Speaker. The government has presented this bill to the House in a spirit of confrontation. How does it expect the workers of Canada to accept it and then perform beyond what is required of them when takeovers are taking place, excessive profits are being made and CP steamships are flying the flag of another country and manning its ships with workers from another country? All this is in the interest of profit and not in the spirit of building Canada. Yet the workers of Canada are being asked to try to help rebuild. The government's policies have destroyed Canada. In a manufacturing economy we have to start to build and put things back together. We have to hire employees, invest in the unemployed and put them back to work.
I should like to talk about other things that have taken place with the railway trade unions, Mr. Speaker. There is the problem of the grievance procedure. Who is going to devote his time to a local grievance committee which is 100, 200 or 300 miles away from the general chairman? This job of representing 200 or 300 employees carries no remuneration. Safety problems such as those with the Connaught tunnel where exhaust fumes overtook some employees and resulted in their being taken to hospital in the past cannot be discussed at a distance. A bill such as this requires that a monetary value be


placed on such incidents, and then it is declared to be a monetary issue and the workers are told to find the best solution they can to the problem.
I want to talk about train derailments on the CNR, CP Rail and the other railways. Employees go out to try to clear the track and get the trains moving again. Some of them work as long as 24 or 36 hours without rest in wet, cold and miserable conditions. An agreement has been signed, sealed and delivered by the unions and companies and voted on by the membership, yet legislation can take it away. Is that democracy? I call it hypocrisy.
Those are the things that this bill will do, Mr. Speaker. It will destroy the basis on which we have built a free collective bargaining system. 1 should have liked to ask the chief mediation officer, Mr. Kelly, for whom railway workers have the deepest respect, if he had been allowed to come to the committee, how he was going to deal with some of these problems. I would have liked to ask the labour relations officer who came to Revelstoke to investigate an illegal dispute over hours of work and meals on the job about all these things.
The grain people were blaming the railway workers and the railway workers were blaming the railways, while the truth of the matter was that so much traffic was coming in from the coalfields in the Kootenays, there was so much grain, so much potash and so much sulphur all arriving together, that the workers had reached their limit.
The labour relations officer went to investigate. The workers defied the law and they were told that although their problems were recognized they would have to wait until their bargaining unit went through the proper process. They pleaded with the judge and told him that they realized they had broken the law but they had to bring the issue to someone's attention. However, they were fined $500 each under the Canada Labour Code. Now the Canada Labour Code is going to be butchered in half. How are you going to have accountability from mediation officers, labour relations officers and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) when the President of the Treasury Board starts bringing in legislation that he knows nothing about? He denies the committee the right to have the Minister of Labour and his officials appear before that committee.
I want to say, and I say it with the deepest of thoughts, that I can see some very, very serious problems arising as a result of this legislation. I hope I am wrong. I hope to goodness I am wrong. We have had a free collective bargaining system working which recognized the cost of living. Our trade unions have operated in a responsible way and have said: "We recognize the problem; therefore, we will not put in our demands. But at the end if there is a cost of living clause, we expect to get it." People have been getting the cost of living increases. But what is going to happen in January when these workers are not only told that their wages on which they have a signed contract will be rolled back but also that their COLA clause has been destroyed? If the cost of living continues to rise, what
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
do you think is going to happen, Mr. Speaker? I can see the framework within each local union starting to disintegrate.
Why would anyone in their right mind want to take a position on a local trade union when his hands would be tied behind his back? How do you think this person would feel when he is faced by literally 200 or 300 members who plead for something to be done? Members approach their union representative on faith. You hear them say "I have my ten hours in; I want to get home. I was in Field for over 14 hours, I want to get home." Who in their right mind would take on those kinds of responsibilities?
When the AIB guidelines were in force, some of those things were recognized. They were serious. You cannot and you must not dictate policies when you have had the freedom of collective bargaining.
The trade union movement, especially in the railways, has come a long way working with the Ministry of Labour, working with various departments, whether in mediation, in conciliation or in labour relations. People had a feeling they would be heard. When things fail, there was a railway arbitration system to which they could go. People accept decisions of arbitrators. Yet almost 90 per cent of the time the arbitrator rules in favour of the company, but people accept these decisions because they were made through an arbitration system. Representatives of the railways, the labour unions and companies come to an agreement and they accept the arbitrator's decision. They feel that at least their case was heard.
How many cases will get that far now? The local process will be gone. The general chairman's authority will be criticized by every worker who will say: "You can do nothing for me. The bill is in front of us. Everything is tied up. What can you do for us? The law has been passed. We are severely dealt with. Where do we go from here?" Those are the kinds of problems this bill will create.
There is one more myth which I would like to refer to before I close. It concerns productivity. I refer to the U.S. bureau of labour statistics which in 1981 stated that hourly wages in manufacturing were 11 per cent lower in Canada than in the United States. Let us look at longer-term figures. Let us take a look at ten major western nations, including Canada. Every single country had higher manufacturing wage increases than Canada between 1975 and 1980. Here is the list: in Great Britain, manufacturing wage increases top 115 per cent; Prance up 104 per cent; Belgium up 100 per cent; Italy up 93 per cent; Japan up 93 per cent; West Germany up 91 per cent; Holland up 85 per cent; Sweden 76 percent; the United States up 56 per cent, and Canada up 48 per cent. Canadian workers are not pricing themselves out of the market. That is a myth which this government and the Conservative Party are trying to spell out across Canada. I think it is time the government started to deal with the serious problems of our economy. The government should not be taking it out on the workers and stealing money from the workers' pockets.

I challenge members of the opposition to get behind this measure so that we as Canadians can get inflation down, can maintain our competitive position in international markets, and can avoid the corporate liquidity crisis which we are facing. These are the three reasons that I believe this six and five bill is necessary.
It is also important that the bill be equitable. We have heard criticism from the opposition that we are picking on public servants, that they are the only ones who will be bearing the burden of the fight against inflation. Members of the opposition forget their own rhetoric. They forget the fact that small businesses have been bearing a very heavy burden in the fight against inflation. They forget that farmers have been bearing a very heavy burden in the fight against inflation. They forget that labour in the private sector, far from being able to obtain a raise of 6 per cent, are losing their jobs. They forget that home owners are having to renew their mortgages at rates which put a tremendous strain on their budgets, at tremendous


sacrifice to them. The public service is not the only one bearing the brunt.
We must keep in mind that there is much greater job security in the public service. This is not something we have to back up with statistics because we know it, but it can be backed up statistically. There is much greater job security in the public sector than in the private sector. In exchange for that job security, we are asking that the increases-not cutbacks-in the salaries be limited to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the following year. Many public servants in my riding are supporting this measure. In fact, I can count on one hand the number of complaints I have received. I have had more telephone calls of support. As most of my colleagues will know, it is rare that people will telephone in support of anything. Usually they are telephoning to complain. That is the general case, and as Members of Parliament we all know it.
On this issue people are telephoning us in support because they want some direction. They want to see the government taking a direct course of action which will have positive results in the near term, because they know that time is critical. For the first time in the last year we have seen representatives of business supporting the measures of government. We have seen bankers supporting measures. Even the occasional media person has supported them. People are beginning to realize that it is time we stopped this conspiracy of negativism that everything is wrong, that everything the government has done is wrong, that everything the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does is wrong. People do not buy that any more. They want to see constructive action.
Despite the lack of popularity of the Liberal Party at this time, of which we are all aware, this measure has received support because it is a good one and it gives direction. People in their intuition are sensing that we are on the road to turning the economy around.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to be participating in this, the debate at the report stage of Bill C-124, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada. My pleasure, though, is not derived from any sense that the bill is a good one. In fact, the legislation is not only bad; it is also grossly unfair.
I say unfair because the bill discriminates wildly against one group of workers in the country, namely public employees, by forcing them to carry virtually single-handedly the burden of the government's restraint program. Maximum permissible increases in wage rates for them are to be set at 6 per cent in the first year of application and 5 per cent in the second, regardless of whether an individual is a $14,000 a year janitor or a $75,000 a year deputy minister.
Equally offensive to my party is that the principle of collective bargaining, including the right to strike, is being effectively suspended in a most unfair way as the government moves to impose unilaterally conditions of employment on its own employees.
We are now debating Motion No. 4. Regarding that motion, we on this side accept the principle of restraint embodied in the bill, even to the extent of the proposed 6 per cent and 5 per cent ceilings. We think that while increases in the total payroll of the public service should not exceed those percentages, collective bargaining rights should be retained to resolve issues like the particular pay packet of individual employees, as well as health, safety, grievances and other general issues.
My party does not object to the government's goal of restraining wages and prices in Canada to combat inflation. Indeed, we have been pressing the government all along to act, especially in the area of curbing its own voracious appetite to spend taxpayers' money. What we object to most in Bill C-124, however, is the arbitrary way the government has decided to impose restraint.
There are essentially two problems. There are others, but there are two in particular. First, the government has singled out public employees to bear the lion's share of the burden of the restraint program, as if, magically, by restraining their salaries alone, inflation would somehow automatically recede. Secondly, even within the public service, the burden will be borne unevenly from one employee to another, for the program is essentially regressive.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to deal first with the fact that public employees are being asked to carry more than their share. Public employees constitute a relatively small proportion of the total work force-conventional wisdom notwithstanding. The government's program applies to employees in line departments of government, to Members of Parliament and senators and their staffs, to employees of Crown corporations, to the RCMP, to judges, and to Armed Forces personnel. In all, some
500,000	people are affected.
I admit that this number is not insignificant but the total is small compared to the whole work force in the country, which numbered 12,192,000 in June, if I remember correctly. Even if the salary of every public employee in the country was slashed to $1, inflation would not disappear. Obviously, the government believes it needs a convenient whipping boy to blame for its mismanagement of the economy and to demonstrate that it has finally converted to restraint. Therefore, the public service is being made the scapegoat.
Once again we have evidence that the government is motivated, not by the public interest but by its own narrow, partisan interest. Opinion polls have demonstrated that civil servants are currently out of favour with the public. Highly publicized strikes in certain sectors, notably at the post office, and among air traffic controllers and others, have left a bitter taste with many people throughout the land. It does not matter, it seems, that most labour disputes in the public sector are settled amicably and without strikes. Unfortunately, the image of public employees is, unfairly I submit, at an all-time low. True to form, the government thinks that it can reverse its


plummeting fortunes coast to coast by flexing its muscles at the expense of the public service. Doctor Gallup and Mr. Goldfarb have told the government that those people are unpopular, so the government has decided to do battle with them in order to court public favour. That is exactly what Bill C-124 is all about. It is a public relations job.
After spending the country into bankruptcy during the last 14 years, the government has suddenly chosen to make restraint the rallying cry in its fight to win back public support. People can see behind the facade of this feigned conversion. They instinctively and intuitively recognize the essential unfairness of it all. The government is slapping 6 per cent and
5	per cent ceilings on allowable salary increases in the public service, no matter what the income level might be in a particular case.
For the high rollers at the upper levels of the income ladder,
6	per cent would mean an allowable increase of $4,000 or more, which is not a small bundle even in these times of debased currency. By contrast, the lowly junior secretary or maintenance person who receives 6 per cent on a $14,000 salary gets a paltry $840, which is hardly enough to pay the daycare bill of a single parent for half a year.
1 wholeheartedly agree with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who said during her excellent speech on Friday, that people at the lower end of the salary scale should be allowed a higher percentage increase than those at the upper end. In this respect, I would perhaps go even further. 1 believe the low-income group should be permitted increases on a sliding scale, beginning with something close to a full cost of living adjustment at the very lowest level. All these matters could be considered, within the constraints of the over-all 6 per cent and 5 per cent ceiling, through the normal collective bargaining system and not imposed on by the government on the public service. In this manner allowable increases could be less as one went up the income ladder. Obviously, increases could not be too great, except at the lower level, because the general 6 per cent and 5 per cent restraint ceiling must be respected. But in the case of the highest paid public servants-those earning $50,000 or more-salaries could be held down and perhaps even close to the existing levels. In a sense, such an approach applies the principle of the progressive income tax system by calling on the strongest among us to carry the heaviest load.
As the amendment at present before us and the amendments to be introduced later by our party later contemplate, the approach that I have in mind will help spread the sacrifice to be made in the name of restraint more evenly while preserving the cherished principle of collective bargaining. Rather than a scheme being imposed on the public service by the government, individual salary ranges and other matters such as health benefits-if consistent with the over-all objective of 6 per cent and 5 per cent limits-could be worked out following careful negotiations between both sides, instead of being imposed on one side by the other.
Of the 215,643 regular full-time employees of the federal government, which does not include employees of Crown corporations or other such agencies although they are also
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
covered under Bill C-124, 13 per cent earn less than $15,000, about 40 per cent earn less that $20,000, while well over half-60 per cent to be exact-earn less than $25,000. In all, 75 per cent earn less than $30,000. That is not a lot of money.
These figures belie the widespread notion that public employees are highly paid. They are not. Most of them are struggling with the same kind of income-related pressures faced by virtually everyone else in society. The problem is particularly acute for women in the public service. While 39 per cent of the total number of men in this sector earn $23,000 or under, 79 per cent of the total of women earn $23,000 or under. In its present form, Bill C-124 will perpetuate inequities such as this.

speechtext:
It is a great area, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has rightly pointed out. There are many federal public employees in that riding in addition to provincial civil servants. I know many of them personally and others at least as acquaintances. My work as an MP requires me to work hand in hand with these people and their counterparts elsewhere in the Atlantic region, especially in regional head offices, and in Ottawa. My experience is that public employees are the most maligned group in society and no doubt partly due to their own deficiencies in the public relations area. They could be doing a great deal more than they are to present themselves as the hardworking, industrious and resourceful people they are in fact. Nevertheless, they are commonly perceived as being underworked, overpaid and too plentiful for all the good they do. However, the truth is that we in Canada have the best public service in the world, with the possible exception of Britain from which our public service has inherited its traditions of dedication and professionalism.
In my view, the extent to which the public service is taken for granted by Canadians is, in reality, a measure of how efficiently our public employees do their job; unobtrusively yet competently. By the same token, only when they are on strike, which is rare, do we sometimes realize how dependent we are on the services these fine people provide. Sure, there are exceptions, just as there are in any enterprise, be it public or private. Understandably, there will be more such underachievers in government, if government is the largest employer in a given community, just by virtue of their large presence in that community. But 1 know that, proportionately, government harbours as many diligent, competent and qualified employees as can be found in any field in the country. I defy anyone to demonstrate otherwise.
That, 1 think, is in the spirit of the motions that we are now debating at report stage of the debate on Bill C-124. Many people would be amazed to learn, as I have through my work,


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
how effectively public employees actually perform, frequently well beyond the call of duty. By requiring public employees to bear the lion's share of the burden of the government's restraint program, instead of including them in an over-all package of wage and price restraint, sensitive to the low-income people in particular, the government is both reflecting and contributing to the conventional myth that those people are responsible for the double-digit inflation in the country. Nothing could be further from the truth. The blame for our inflation, the blame for our unemployment, the blame for our debased dollar, the blame for investment capital fleeing our country from coast to coast, rests squarely with the political mismanagers in the federal cabinet, especially the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who has been calling the shots for the last 14 years.
At the heart of the inflation problem, in particular, has been the government's 14-year spending spree which has seen government expenditures soar an incredible 630 per cent since the Prime Minister took office in 1968. The deficit of the federal government this year is several billion dollars more, probably as high as $7 billion more, than the total budget of the government in the Prime Minister's first year in office. Having increased its total spending this past year by some 20 per cent, having racked up a deficit of $19.6 billion in the current year alone, 80 per cent higher than forecast as recently as seven months earlier, the government now expects everyone, public servants and the general public alike, to settle for no more than 6 per cent and 5 per cent increases in their salaries.
Nothing else has contributed to inflationary pressures in Canada as much as has the government's overspending. That overspending is largely the result of the establishment of costly programs like metric which the public neither wants nor needs, as well as waste in the administration of programs which the public does want and does need. Little of the overexpenditure relates to bloated salaries of public employees or their numbers, except at the highest levels.
What we need is a resolve by the government, throughout the cabinet, to devise a total economic package, including low interest rates, to get people producing, selling and working again. Only when the one million unemployed in Canada are back in the labour force earning salaries, only when they are gainfully employed and paying income tax on those salaries, will we see a marked reduction in the federal deficit and in the multibillion dollar costs of our current unemployment insurance and welfare programs. The government should be attacking the unemployment problem in the country. Instead, it is attacking public employees whose formidable skills should be marshalled with those of the private sector in a real war against the serious economic crisis facing us all.

What we are trying to do with this bill is to get ourselves to the point where the inflation rate in this country is brought down to 6 per cent or 7 per cent. Some say this bill will not do that. Certainly it will not. This bill is the government's start in that direction. If the government does not do this, then why would anyone else? One has to give an example, to make a start.
If, and I am hopeful this "if' will come true, we are successful in convincing other sectors of the Canadian economy that this is the right direction and wages, prices and inflation are brought down, at that time the 6 per cent and 7 per cent will be the cost of living. Therefore, public servants should not suffer any more than the rest of the population. This is a reasonable approach to this situation.
There is no simple single answer. That is what H. L, Menken was saying when he was dealing with the Scope trial. That is what a lot of economists are saying today. There is not one simple thing you can do quickly. You cannot just spend more, gut the National Energy Program and all your problems will be solved. This is a very complex and dangerous period internationally in terms of economics. The simple act of passing this bill will not really solve all the problems. It is an indication that we want to start solving the problems.
We on this side, and I am sure those on the other side, are concerned about the serious difficulty we have to face, high interest rates. There is a very definite relationship between high interest rates and the rate of inflation. The term "real interest" is the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate. Traditionally that rate in terms of bank prime should be between 2 per cent and 3 per cent over an historical period of time. That rate is probably 7 or 8 per cent in the United States and 5 or 6 per cent in Canada. It varies depending on the inflation rate and, of course, changes in the interest rate.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
Real interest rates are too high; no one says they are not. They should come down. In order to change interest rates significantly, we must bring down the inflation rate. If we get the inflation rate down to 6 or 7 per cent, then we can move. If the expectation is that it will stay down, we can move to considerably lower interest rates. That will have a tremendously stimulating effect on the economy.
This will not be accomplished by any simple means. It was very nice in the fifties and sixties when we could depend on Keynes. We could take some fiscal or monetary measures to stimulate the economy or slow it down, depending on the condition it was in. It was very simple and we could achieve considerable results. We were not always as successful as we might have been, but that was not because of Keynes. In most countries it was because the timing was off a bit.
That does not work any more. The failure of this to work, the reliance on simplistic answers, the simple need but wrong answers that we hear, show that it is that reliance that is wrong. There are some things we can begin to do, and this is one of them.
We often hear that the cause of the problem is government spending. As the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) stated earlier, the country with the highest spending in relation to its gross national product is Japan, yet that country has the lowest inflation and interest rates of all industrial nations. There are many reasons which indicate that huge government deficits are not the basic problems that we are facing.
This year we are going to have a deficit of close to $20 billion. It might be a little lower or a shade higher, but it will be in that area. In November it was projected the deficit would be about $10.5 billion. It climbed very rapidly in the last eight months.
The reason for the climb is not an increase in government spending. There has been some increase. Eighty cents of every dollar of that increase in the deficit has been directly due to decreased government revenues. Twenty cents of that dollar is due to increased government expenditures, mostly caused by a world recession. It has been because of a decline in revenue. Most of the increased expenditures have been caused by a global recession. It is not a simple matter to deal with.
Government spending is not the major source of all of the problem. This government will spend approximately $90 billion in the next fiscal year. Only 20 per cent of that amount will be spent on the operation of government, the part this bill deals with, although we are dealing outside of the public sector when we deal with those areas under the Canada Labour Code, as indicated in this motion.
Only 20 per cent of government spending is for the operation of government; defence, the post office, and all other operations of government. The other 80 per cent is transferred to Canadians in one way or another either through the provinces, directly to Canadians through pensions, or in other ways. We should have a good debate in this House about where the money comes from, where it goes and whether that is the way it should be done, rather than a debate on the


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
amount. Governments such as in Sweden and other countries transfer perhaps 50 per cent of their gross national product from one group to another. That is the debate we should be having. The amount of the transfer is not all that significant.
Again with regard to these simplicities we keep running into, I would like to compare our situation with that in the United States. Not long ago I was criticized for talking about the United States rather than Canada. The economy of this country for many reasons is tremendously dependent on the economy of the United States. One reason is the very large ownership factor. That was one of the reasons we brought in the National Energy Program, which the Tories would love to be rid of. Before that program was brough in, 75 per cent of our oil and gas resources were owned offshore, mostly by American companies. That was a very good reason why we brought in the national energy policy, and it is a very good reason to talk about the American economy and compare it with ours. I think that comparison is important.
One of the statements often made since the budget is that our deficit as a percentage of our gross national product is double the American deficit. That simply is not true. As a percentage of gross national product our deficit is about the same as the American deficit will be. There is a very small difference between the two deficits. The American deficit is $100 billion; we can probably say that is a close estimate, but the American deficit will not be $100 billion in the fiscal year coming up, it will be in the area of $160 billion to $170 billion. The total deficits of both countries will be approximately the same in terms of gross national product. Sometimes we use the ten to one ratio. The ten to one ratio is not adequate because our gross national product is larger than that of the United States. The ten to one ratio does not quite work. However, the deficits of the two countries are very, very similar.
One of the interesting things about the government's deficit is the deficit as a function of savings. The total Canadian gross national product will be about $360 billion in the current fiscal year. The government deficit of $20 billion represents about 5.1 per cent of the total gross national product. At the same time, Canadians have a gross capital formation-savings-in the order of 25 per cent of our gross national product.
I obviously do not like simplicity in this regard, but let me make a simple comparison. A family which spends something in the order of $2,000 more than it earns but actually saves $9,000 in another way is not in bad shape. Basically speaking, if we look at the Canadian economy and see the deficit at $20 billion but our gross capital formation at $90 billion, then we do not see that deficit as being so serious that we cannot live with it. That represents something like 21 per cent or 22 per cent of capital formation. In the United States the figure is closer to 30 per cent. Canadian problems in this respect are not more serious than American problems. They are problems, however, in terms of inflation.
Our inflation rate is still a good deal higher than the American inflation rate. It is probably three or four percentage points higher. It is hard to tell because the American rate has
been fluctuating quite a bit in the past couple of months. The American rate has been up considerably, but one can assume about a 4 per cent to 5 per cent difference in the rates. That is the problem this bill and this motion attempt to ease so that we can get interest rates down.
In this comparison there is one area on which we have not spent much time. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is one who can accept a lot of praise for her efforts in this respect. As a country we have not cut back significantly-we have not really cut back at all-the amount of money we provide for social services. There has been a very small cut in the old age pension. It is not really a cut; it is a reduction of the increase to 6 per cent for people who presumably have sufficient funds. It is not a cut for those who do not.
I would like to relate a short story about the situation in the United States to give some idea of what is happening there. In the middle of June President Reagan went to Texas and spoke at a testimonial dinner for the governor of Texas. Thirty-five hundred people came out to that testimonial dinner to hear their president, and each laid out $1,000 a plate for this dinner. In the same week that those 3,500 Americans-from Texas, mostly-laid out $1,000 each for a meal, the state of Texas put out a brochure indicating that people should not move to that state because there was a high unemployment rate in the south, particularly in Texas, because with no national energy program the oil industry was in serious trouble throughout the United States. That very week the state of Texas put out a brochure which said that people on welfare would get monthly incomes of $32 for food stamps and an additional $32. That is in a country where 3,500 people are able to lay out $1,000 each for a single meal.
The Government of Canada has not at any stage forgotten its social responsibilities. This government has not reduced expenditures for health, welfare and so forth. We are not cutting these things back. I noted that the social council gave some praise to the government for not doing that. I think that is one of the fundamental differences in the two countries. If this recession becomes worse, the base for any kind of recovery will be the fact that we are funnelling out money for unemployment insurance benefits, solving social problems and making sure people have some money to buy goods.
I could go into much more detail on the American scene than I have done. I am very much afraid that base is disappearing in the United States.
Hon. members opposite offer simple solutions to our problems. As Menken says, they look at a complex problem and come up with a simple, neat, wrong answer. I say this bill is a beginning. It is with this bill that we start to come together as Canadians to reduce our inflation. That is one step. There have to be many steps to solve the problems this country and the rest of the world face.

I suggest to the hon. member that if we were to raise our energy price to 75 per cent of world price tomorrow, our inflation would start coming down. It is a ridiculous situation but that is exactly what would happen. The inflation rate would descend and the expectations of higher inflation would also descend.
I think we can accept the fact that three or four percentage points of inflation will still be caused by energy prices. I do not

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians must be wondering why the House has been sitting practically all summer. Well, I hope they realize that the present government is doing everything it possibly can to remedy the present economic situation.
Obviously, Bill C-124 is not a panacea. In any case, Mr. Speaker, I do not think any parliament, whether here in Canada or anywhere else in the world, has ever been able to come up with the ideal solution to all our ills. We do not claim that this measure is going to be effective on all counts but, as I said before, none of the laws passed by the world's parliaments has ever been perfect. Take old age security, for instance. If we had wanted to be absolutely fair, there are millionaires who certainly do not need the pension and there are other people who need it very badly, so it is impossible to come up with a measure that will please everyone.
Of course, my colleagues opposite-and I am not surprised, since they are fond of criticizing-are opposed to this bill and have said so during the hours this House has been considering this legislation. On the other hand, they have been unable to come up with any tangible solutions. These people are fence-sitters, because they are trying to please everybody. However, there comes a time, Mr. Speaker, when a responsible government must make decisions that, though not necessarily attractive to everyone, are aimed at correcting certain situations. Of course, the New Democratic Party especially is fiercely opposed to this measure to restrict wage increases. We must not forget, however-and I think everyone will agree, the members of the New Democratic Party as well-that the main problem, and this is nothing new, the main problem is, how are we going to fight inflation? We are also agreed that there is a price to pay if we want to fight inflation. And we know that this price is being paid today by the people who are being laid off: the last to be hired are the first to be fired. This price is also being paid by businessmen who are faced with high interest rates and are daily running the risk of losing their shirt. So there is a price to pay, and these are the people who are now paying the price for bringing inflation down to more rational proportions. So what do we do with the public service
19972


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
where people have practically absolute job security? Is the government supposed to go on handing out wage increases of up to 11 or 12 per cent and let these people who have job security take advantage of the fact that others have to pay the price for bringing inflation down to more rational proportions? Should we let them be a burden to the unemployed and to businessmen who are going bankrupt? Is the government supposed to turn around and give more to people with job security? Is it going to say, "Take your wage increase and take advantage of the fact that others are being squeezed dry in order to reduce inflation? Mr. Speaker, I feel that a Liberal government that has always been proud of the fact that the Liberal Party stands for justice, equity and sharing, would have failed in its duty to the country had it done so.
The reason why Canadians keep re-electing Liberal governments is that the Liberal Party stands up for everyone, for the rich and the poor and the middle class. It stands for justice. That is why we cannot afford to have something like this happen. Of course, if the economy were in very good shape, we certainly would not bother putting restrictions on wage increases. Unfortunately, it is like Petula Clark says in her song: Everyone wants to go to heaven but nobody wants to die! Everybody realizes that these are difficult times, but when they are asked to do their bit, they always want the other person to make the effort.
Of course, we must start somewhere. The New Democratic Party members opposite are saying that if we want to control wages, we should control prices as well. It sounds great, but we must not forget that we are living in a free enterprise and competitive society where prices practically control themselves. My colleagues opposite seem to think this is ridiculous. Well, if a perfect solution could be found, I would be the first to look for it. There is some talk of controlling prices; now, I am not necessarily against price controls, on the contrary. If there were a scientifically proven and effective way to control prices,
I would be the first to try it. Unfortunately, introduce price controls and you open up a whole can of worms. And 1 mean it, Mr. Speaker. For instance, people are complaining that CMHC housing is going up, and during question period we are constantly being urged to control the price of homes and control rents to keep increases at 6 per cent or less.
1 would like to remind these people that Canada is a trading country and that CMHC is in the housing business. Of course we could promise not to raise the price of houses by more than 6 per cent, even if that meant we would have the largest deficit ever. We cannot go bankrupt since we are the government. What I mean is, we are competing with the people in the private sector. What is going to happen? We are going to put these people out of business. They will not be able to survive if the government gives them unfair competition. It is unfair because as a government we can absorb deficits indefinitely, but how can we expect the small entrepreneur, who is already
losing money if he only raises prices by 9 or 10 per cent, to stay in business if he is restricted to 6 per cent? We have to remember that sort of thing. It sounds wonderful, this clamouring for price controls as well as wage controls, but it is not as easy as it sounds.
Mr. Speaker, I wish Canadians, and not just the people opposite, but Canadians in general, would give some serious thought to what the consequences would be if the government were to impose price controls in all areas. Obviously, if all our businesses were to go bankrupt as a result of excessive controls-it is not that I like to see companies making exorbitant profits, certainly not-but if price controls are excessive, we may be causing companies to go bankrupt. I really doubt that would be in the interest of Canadian workers.
I think that, generally speaking Canadians realize that a start has to be made somewhere, and we on the government side have decided to set an example and start putting our own house in order. We are often accused of minding everybody's business except our own, Mr. Speaker, but I think most governments have this habit of minding other people's business. But this time, it is our business, and it is up to the government to do something about it. The government is responsible for the public service and all Crown corporations, and therefore, in a situation like the one existing today, the government must act. Most public servants agree wholeheartedly with this measure. Of course, Mr. McDermott and the New Democratic Party and cohorts do not agree, but most public servants do. They know perfectly well that this is not a punitive measure, it is anything but, and it is not because we want to impose anything on anyone or because we resent anyone but, as I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, it would be absolutely unfair in our present society for people to be laid off while others enjoy absolute job security and are being granted more money.
Mr. Speaker, if I were a public servant and were earning $12,000 or $15,000 a year, in the circumstances I would rather have my salary increase restricted to 6 per cent than get my 11 per cent increase and be obliged to go on unemployment insurance or welfare. So I want to make it quite clear to all public servants that this is not a punitive measure, on the contrary. We realize that we are working closely with public servants, some of whom are our employees, and we want to treat them with dignity and respect. Of course, some people are going to be rather pleased because like the politicians, the bureaucracy is not necessarily well loved, and it was Balzac who said that the bureaucracy was a monster administered by pygmies. In fact, Mr. Speaker, although many Canadians may see the bureaucracy as a monster, these people often work, without recognition, to enhance the well-being of the entire population. So, these people understand perfectly our position and our reasons for taking this action.
Mr. Speaker, a start had to be made somewhere, and everyone knows that here in Canada we have had some very


good and prosperous years, and we have lived very well. Now we are going through a difficult period, and people should realize that they will have to make an effort to change their lifestyle. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I hope my colleagues will go outside to talk if they are not too much in a hurry; if they really want to talk maybe they could talk outside, it is a bit disturbing, Mr. Speaker, so 1 would say that a country's economic ups and downs are very similar to the human life or cycle, also just like in the bush: when there is a population explosion of certain animals and then there is an epidemic and they die and the situation goes back to normal. It is about the same in an economy. In good years, businessmen make more profits, they are more generous when business is good and give more substantial wage increases until they realize that they can no longer do so. The economy cannot always follow an upward trend. At some point, you have to face the facts, and this is what happens then.
We have to realize that we may have expected a bit too much. We have a population of 24 million people in Canada and there are 28 million credit cards in circulation. It will give food for thought to many people to know that 28 million credit cards are in circulation and that we have a debt of $200,000 per capita, for every one of our 24 million people, and that the child who is born today has a debt of $200,000. This is the federal, provincial, municipal and corporate debt. It amounts to $200,000 per capita.
I would like to know what opposition members believe would be a normal, acceptable debt for a country like ours. Of course, they will suggest something else because, generally speaking, members of the opposition wait to see what we are about to suggest. They like to play cat and mouse. As soon as we speak up to suggest something, they are against it. If we had suggested something else or made an alternative proposal, they would have recommended the very thing to which they are now opposed. It is obvious that the members opposite have no really constructive proposals to make, but they still stay in the House and delay passage of this bill without reason.
Mr. Speaker, we in the government can always intervene, but each time we do, it is an artificial intervention. We can only postpone the crunch and Canadians are beginning to understand it. Canadians throughout the country are now realizing that each time governments intervene by granting a subsidy here and a subsidy there to help such or such a company to remain in business, to prevent it from going into receivership or from closing its doors and to save jobs, it is a good thing for that specific company, but it is unfair to another one which is well managed. Every time the federal or provincial governments intervene, their intervention is artificial. Canadians generally must apply self-discipline. There are limits to the extent to which governments can put bread in the mouths of each individual. We shall now have to realize that we have had good years and that we must now make an effort and lower the thermostat by one degree if need be to make both ends meet. We shall have to work intelligently, the way it is being done now in European countries.
