In the past, Canadian businessmen, for instance, wanted to become millionaires within two years. This is all very well if you can afford it. It does not work like that in Europe. A businessman must stand behind his counter for years. Those are the facts! Workers will also have to be a bit more productive. Employers and businessmen will have to reduce their expenses.
I was in business myself and there were times when money was scarce and I had to get rid of certain items. I was sorry to do so because I thought, "Well, this pickup is nearly paid for and I have to sell it." However, that is what it means to go through a difficult period. Mr. Speaker, I know that the House will pass Bill C-124 this evening and that Canadians in general will understand exactly our position and our decision and I am certain that it will benefit the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain that Bill C-124 which is before us today will be seen by history as an injust bill, as a hollow gesture at fighting inflation. It will be seen as a bill which attempted to make scapegoats of public employees and other working people in Canada for the disastrous economic policies pursued by the government. It will be seen as a bill through which the government, cheered on by Conservative pretenders in opposition, deliberately sparked a confrontation with labour to deflect attention from the destructive impact of high interest rates, rapidly increasing energy costs, and monopoly control of the marketplace in the Canadian economy. Obviously my colleagues in this party and I stand opposed to the bill. The government has forced it upon the people of Canada and we have no intention of letting it slip by without doing everything in our power to attack the inequities of this contemptible piece of legislation and to support whatever constructive amendments are proposed.
My friends to the right, the Tories, seem to be stumbling over themselves to help the government sell this PR campaign. It is a campaign to try to convince Canadians that attacking collective bargaining and the incomes of working people is what is needed to fight inflation. The government is spoiling for a fight with labour to convince Canadians that it is doing something about the economic crisis. The Tories over here are right behind them, trying to limit the ability of working people to fight back within the realm of the law. Unlike the Conservatives, I do not support attacking the living standards of a typist in Winnipeg who earns $11,353 per year, or the people working in government hospitals who earn only $11,055 per year, in order to encourage Ian Sinclair and his blue chip cronies to take advantage of the 6 per cent world of recovery. That is what the bill is intended to do. Neither do I support an attack on the collective bargaining rights of working people in Canada in order to deflect attention from the government's ruinous economic policies.


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) has moved a number of amendments, seeking to reintroduce real collective bargaining in the bill. The effect of his amendments is to return to those people covered under the bill the right, according to the Canada Labour Code or the Public Service Staff Relations Act, to negotiate a collective agreement and the right to choose between arbitration and strike action to solve disputes which may arise in negotiations. These amendments are constructive ones. They restore not just the appearance of collective bargaining but the very substance of it.
The announcement last Thursday by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) that collective bargaining would soon be permitted in the 6 per cent world of relapse was a crafty piece of public relations, but as we have seen, it really lacks the substance to deal with the charge that the government is undermining collective bargaining in Canada. With limits of 6 per cent and 5 per cent on all forms of pay, benefits and prerequisites, there is very little room for negotiation. All the President of the Treasury Board has given the people of the public service is the privilege of negotiating how their standard of living and working conditions will deteriorate, and then only if the government decides to permit negotiations.
According to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), that little statement by the President of the Treasury Board will go a long way toward quelling Tory opposition to the bill. When we scratch the surface, we find that there is really not much Tory opposition to wage controls. Just like their opposition to government economic mismanagement, the Tory opposition to wage controls is a bit of a paper tiger. There is very little to differentiate the Liberals from the Tories in respect of collective bargaining or their remedies for high interest rates, high unemployment and falling productivity in Canada. The Liberals and the Tories want to reintroduce the appearance of collective bargaining rights in the federal public service. That is all it is-the appearance of collective bargaing.
There is precious little for women working for the government who look forward to decent maternity leave provisions. There is precious little for those public service employees nearing retirement who hope for reconsideration of the restraint which will be imposed on their pension incomes. There is nothing for those people hoping for a return to their right .to collective bargaining.
What is the purpose of this bill? When he introduced it four weeks ago, the President of the Treasury Board moaned about the 25 per cent to 30 per cent of our productive capacity standing idle. He complained about the one and one-quarter million people unable to find work, and he gnashed his teeth over the businesses and consumers staggering under high interest rates. We must improve our production, he said; and 1 cannot think of anyone who would disagree with him. Our economy is being ravaged by this recession-cum-depression. It is a dismal picture and it is a picture that we in this corner have been trying to get the government to see for a long time.
We have no doubt it is the ruinous fiscal and monetary policies of this government and the Bank of Canada which have brought this recession upon the heads of Canadians, and the government knows that. It has known that would happen all along. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself has admitted that the object of his government's economic policies is to scare the wits out of Canadians with high unemployment, to reduce their demands on the Canadian economy; and it worked, it did scare the wits out of Canadians, but the only result has been more unemployment, less production and no relief from inflation.
Surely the Liberals cannot be surprised that Canada is now in the grips of a severe recession. They have brought it on intentionally to fight inflation. The Liberal Party, the government of this country, no less than the Tories who snap at their heels, has embraced the monetarist economic policies which are squeezing the life out of western economies everywhere.
The budget introduced in this House on June 28 was a crushing disappointment to the people of Canada. It was a prescription for social chaos and economic disaster. It is another chapter in the decade of Liberal and Conservative economic mismanagement since this crisis began in 1973. This budget held little for Canadians except the same bankrupt principles of monetarism, spiced with a pinch of the voodoo remedies of supply side economics.
The June 28 budget could have been the turning point at which the government abandoned the Conservative economic doctrine of Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher and the Conservative Party of Canada. The government could have turned its back on the unjust economic schemes whose basic tenet is to take from the poor and give to the rich, hoping the rich will be enticed to invest in a more prosperous society. The government could have turned its back on this, but it did not. Instead it gave Canadians a repudiation of the principles of collective bargaining combined with another squeeze on the already falling incomes of ordinary Canadians. It gave Canadians pension cuts and further cutbacks in social services, and so as to sell it the government went scrambling to come up with what it thinks are catchy phrases like solidarity and sharing and a crusade on inflation and the 6 per cent world of recovery.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was preparing his budget he brought in what The Toronto Star called an old Liberal warhorse to advise him on the revolution of semantics. A revolution of semantics, what a lovely phrase! That is the magic that the Liberals expected to sell this thing they call the plan for recovery. For a party that has not had a new idea in ten years I suppose the best thing that they could come up with is a revolution in semantics.
However, I think the Minister of Finance did not quite need to retain an adviser to stage this revolution. At much less cost and with a good deal more honesty he could have borrowed a phrase or two from the 1979 Conservative budget. No less than the Tories, the Liberals' only remedy for the economic


crisis is the short-term pain for long-term gain or rather, to be more honest, it should be short-term gain for long-term pain.
That is what this budget and Bill C-124 are all about: long-term pain for short-term gain. But it is not the $500,000 a year captains of industry and finance who will be hurting; it is the people of this country who work for the government and, after them, those working in the private sector. They are the ones being asked to be the foot soldiers in the government's crusade against inflation. Not only is their real income to be cut over the next two years, but with the limitations imposed on their right to bargain collectively, their working conditions as well could well deteriorate, while they have little power to demand improvements.
1 can see no sense in attacking the wages of working people, wages which have been falling against the cost of living. What makes even less sense is to attack the right to collective bargaining as part of a crusade against inflation. And whether or not the government decides to permit its employees to request negotiations on some parts of their contracts, this bill clearly attacks ferociously their right to collective bargaining under the guise of wage restraint. It is here that the government's logic is most transparent. Attacking collective bargaining may be good sport in the corporate board rooms but in itself the right to bargain collectively really has no impact on inflation.
Last year my party leader received an internal government document spelling out how the government would deal with the economic crisis. Let me quote a paragraph from it. It reads:
A program of consultation and public relations aimed at changing public attitudes and expectations would be useful, even though the main advantage of the program would be that it would enable the government to be seen doing something about inflation and to lay part of the blame for inflation on the private sector.
So that is what the government is doing now. But it is doing so under the rubric of wage controls, laying the blame for inflation not so much on the private sector as on the working people of this country. But even that same document recognizes that it is not wages which are fuelling inflation. That document says this, and I quote again:
We are not currently facing wagedriven inflation such as we were in 1975, instead real wages have fallen for four consecutive years.
That document was written last year. Wages have now fallen for five consecutive years. If wages are not the cause of inflation, and the government apparently recognizes that, can a 6 per cent world of recovery really be an honest attack on inflation? I think not.
Wage controls will not bring inflation down; they will not put people back to work. All they will do is to provoke fresh fights between government and organized labour. Union bashing is a popular avocation among some of Canada's editorial writers and conservative economic think tanks such as the Fraser Institute. With its 6 per cent world of recovery, the Liberal government is trying to woo support from the Conservatives. It is trying to show Conservative supporters it can be every bit as neanderthal, economically, as the Tories can.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
The last time Canadians had a bout with wage controls was from October 1975 to April 1978. Canadians were told that controls were absolutely essential to get the economy off the rocks. They were to be part of a concerted attack on inflation that would put an end to spiralling prices and give the economy a period of stability during which the government promised to do something about unemployment. After 30 months of controls, what did the government accomplish?
When controls were introduced, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) predicted they would bring the inflation rate, which was at 10.6 per cent, down to 4 per cent by 1978. Did they do that? We all know they did not. The rate of inflation in 1978 was not 4 per cent at all, it was 9 per cent. From 1975 to 1978, prices in the country rose by 38.9 per cent, but the control guidelines limited wage increases to only 19 per cent.
What about unemployment? In October, 1975, when controls were introduced, the federal unemployment rate in this country was 7.2 per cent. After 30 months of supposed stability during which the government said it would do something about unemployment, the unemployment rate actually increased to 8.6 per cent. That has to be a discouraging record for the proponents of wage controls, for the Liberals across the floor and for the Conservatives on my right.
The Canadian economy does not need restraint to get back on track. It does not need an attack on collective bargaining. It needs a major shift in economic planning by the government of this country.
Whether the government of this country is formed by Liberals or Conservatives, the only solution Canadians can expect is more long-term pain for short-term gain. The Conservatives are fond of accusing this party of being in collusion with this government, but the record of the House shows that it is the Conservatives who have supported this government's policies most often by votes in this very House. If there is an alliance brewing in this country, it is between the two parties of big business. When it comes to economic planning, the only difference between the two is a difference in style.
Was it not the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who said that the wage controls proposed in the June 28 budget were a step in the right direction? Was it not the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), after accusing the government of being adrift, who admitted that the Tories would not get elected if they now told the public what they would do if they were in government?
What kind of remedy does this Liberal-Tory alliance prescribe for the Canadian economy? They have made the war on inflation their number one priority and have bravely accepted the high and rising levels of unemployment and the farm and small business bankruptcies as the cost of licking inflation. To increase productivity in Canada, they want to strangle the economy with high interest rates, more unemployment and low productivity.
If that is not enough, they want to strangle the economy further by reducing domestic consumption through the imposi-


Business of the House
tion of wage controls and the deindexation of pensions. In both cases their solution rests on a fundamental redistribution of income away from working people and senior citizens, away from farmers and fishermen and from small businesses to the already rich and powerful.
1 think I have made it clear that we find the economic solutions put forward in this bill totally lacking. We find the bill which we are debating today to be unjust. It is a charade designed to hoodwink Canadians into believing the government is doing something positive about the economy. The amendments which we proposed and for which we are asking support of the House later this evening, would only address some of the excesses of Bill C-124. While we believe these amendments should be accepted, we cannot accept the plan for economic recovery that makes working people scapegoats of a government that is trying to get us to believe its hype about a crusade on inflation.

Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for dinner, 1 was about to tell the House how pleased I was to take part in this debate in early August in a session that will certainly turn out to be the longest ever. I want to say why I feel that it is our duty as parliamentarians to be here at the very time, when hundreds of Canadians have an opportunity to come and follow our proceedings and see just how seriously all parties in the House deal with the economic issue. 1 think that all Canadians fully realize that exceptional measures must be taken if we are to come to grips with the crisis that is currently undermining the country. Within the parameters of this debate on Bill C-124, 1 think we must warn all Canadians not to be taken in by such prophets as those of the New Democratic Party who claim to have magic and easy solutions. These are hardly times when irresponsibility, complacency and particularly petty politics are acceptable. I would suggest that the times we are going through are too important for the
1,250,000	idle Canadians who can only hope and entertain the thought that their government does not forget them. The magic solutions advocated by the New Democratic Party simply do not wash in economics or in sociology because, if we were to endorse their theory, everything would be a cinch, we would simply spend more money.
They fail to say where the money would be coming from but, as far as they are concerned, the way out is to spend more money. We heard them during the sittings of the committee when they claimed that the solution is not to cut back the salaries of the public servants, but to give them more money to enable them to spend and keep the economy rolling. If we were to do that, we would find ourselves in a situation where the Canadian people would have to pay a very steep price for a small minority, which happens to be among those who enjoy the best protection in the country. The real issue is that the time may not have come yet for the New Democratic Party to pay its debts to the unions that provide its financing. It would be better to let those unions realize the seriousness of the crisis and enable them to join the collective effort aimed at restoring in Canada an acceptable and profitable level of economic activity for all Canadians. There is no simple formula to curb inflation. To be here today and propose a-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: And the high interest rates?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
If you will remain silent, I will talk about high interest rates later on. I did not interrupt you when you had the floor. Mr. Speaker, we all wish for a higher standard of living, we would all like to see Canadians live in a world of opulence, but the fact is that the standard of living is related to individual responsibility. We often have misconceptions about our wealth. People think that we are going to pull through this crisis because Canada is a wealthy country and that nobody will have to make personal sacrifices, but the reality is something else again. We have been deluding ourselves for the past five, six, seven or eight years by telling one another that the public coffers were bottomless. Today we are faced with the sad reality: Canadians can no longer contribute as generously as in the past to government programs. They simply cannot pay too many taxes and yet, at the same time, they expect the government to come up with solutions. Those who now bear the brunt of the economic crisis are mainly young people and women who make up the majority of the unemployed. They are also businessmen on the brink of bankruptcy because they cannot compete any longer on some markets.
It seems to me that if we went along with what the New Democratic Party is suggesting, the rest of the people would suffer, while unionized civil servants would be protected. It seems to me also that the Canadian people now have neither the means nor the desire to protect anybody. What they want is economic leadership. They want their government and all its elected representatives to lead the way. They rely on firmness and a sincere desire to end the crisis once and for all and to wrestle to the ground this inflation which would destroy us all sooner or later. When Mr. Karl Beigie appeared before our committee, he gave three causes for inflation. He mentioned, of course, that the main cause is increased costs. It is a fact


that energy costs have increased tremendously over the past ten years.
Labour costs have increased as well, and caught in a vicious circle, we say, "Because of the higher cost of living, give us more money without bothering about productivity!" And whenever we get an automatic pay increase of 12 or 13 per cent, does it really reflect an increase in productivity? And we realize that in the past few years in Canada, in spite of significant pay increases in every sector of the economy, there has been no corresponding rise in productivity; in fact, productivity has stagnated. Mr. Beigie felt also that the Canadian dollar in the 50's had been overvalued, although other economists may feel differently; yet, in his view and as he sees economic reality, from the moment the Canadian dollar found its true value, the cost of imported goods increased accordingly and fed inflation. We often hear people say that the value of the Canadian dollar should be set in such a way that it is worth one dollar to Canadians buying on the domestic market. A dollar is always worth a dollar, but because of the great many imports we buy-we have become more sophisticated customers, we appreciate imported and choice cheeses and other similar products-we are, as 1 said, sophisticated consumers, and this also feeds inflation, because our dollar is worth 80 cents U.S. and we import a tremendous amount of goods, this causes costs to rise.
Mr. Beigie referred also to a new phenomenon, namely, state control over increasingly larger areas of the economy. Under popular pressure, probably with the best intentions in the world, governments have taken an active part in the marketplace, have become involved in dozens of social and economic programs of every shape and form which are becoming increasingly costly for the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian economy as a whole. We have also contributed to the spiralling increase in the cost of living by individually and collectively deciding to protect ourselves against it by indexing social benefits to the cost of living; so, we have made monsters of programs which originally were quite modest but are now costing us an arm and a leg, Mr. Speaker, something that is forcing us to lower our expectations. We have to ask ourselves whether Canada can keep on spending, even with the best intentions in the world. But can the Canadian people still afford all those expenditures without complaining; are those expenditures synonymous with growth? We feel that growth can never be achieved unless we change our ways. The last few years have proved it beyond a doubt; unfortunately, that experience has made its victims: we must now turn to those victims, and the government must take drastic measures to remedy the situation.
Salaries, which 1 mentioned a moment ago, no longer bear any relation to productivity; it is a forgotten element of our language, an element none of the unions which came before the committee even mentioned. They merely said: We need more! But they did not relate what they deserve to what they

produce; that notion is unfortunately too often overlooked, which explains our problems in world markets. Yes, over the past five years, our productivity has been stagnating and the cost of labour at all levels of government has increased. We should ask ourselves what the rate of productivity is in government services. With all the resources of his staff, the Auditor General of Canada has assessed the productivity of the public service at 60 per cent compared with the private sector. I do not want to generalize because there are of course public servants who have a productivity of 110 percent. Others, unfortunately, must have a lower than average productivity, which would mean lower than 60 per cent, but none of those who appeared before the committee to speak on behalf of public servants mentioned productivity. I believe that other Canadians are becoming more and more concerned about productivity, whether in the private sector or in some public agencies, and they are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of being more productive if we want to keep our markets open.
The bill now under consideration is really part of a general restraint policy. Parliament has been asked to vote on this matter which is the most urgent of all the legislative and administrative measures put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), because if we want to convince everyone that the government means business, that it wants to practise what it preaches and that we are not just long on rhetoric when we talk about tightening our belts, we have to show the Canadian people that we are going to impose restraint first on ourselves, the members of the House of Commons and the Senate, on our own staff and on the public service in the hope that other public agencies and the private sector will follow our lead to give jobs back to those who need them so much and to bring down inflation, which in turn will bring interest rates down. I am convinced that with this bill we shall lead the way in this fight against inflation. Bill C-124 should be seen rather as a model for all Canadians to copy from. It is but one component of a general policy. If the government were to suggest that Bill C-124 will solve all our problems, I do not think the Canadian people would take it seriously. It is all very well to control wages, but prices too have to be controlled.
The Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) have made many announcements concerning prices because these two factors are interrelated. If we look at the recent announcement made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove)-if my hon. colleague would care to listen and learn, he would see that when the government talks about price control, it does mean business-no rent paid to the Canadian government-and we know how many housing units it controls in Canada-will be increased by more than 6 percent. Many other prices will be regulated and I am already convinced that the same will apply to Bell Canada and many others if we want this program to be effective.

All members of this House have to take this program seriously. If they are here only to score political points, as our colleagues of the New Democratic Party seem to be doing, if they are here to make sure that the program will not work, they are not discharging their responsibilities as the people's representatives who must see to the best interests of the whole population and not just clean up the slate with those who contribute to their party fund. I believe that it is important for all Canadians to realize that the New Democratic Party made no contribution whatsoever to the debate during consideration of the bill in committee. Most of its members did not even vote on the proposed amendments. They did not vote for a very simple reason, they wanted two things: first, to have an unblemished record; second, to pay their debts to the unions which fund them. Gentlemen, you succeeded. Now, Mr. Speaker, we must return to the Progressive Conservative Party which in spite of its differences of opinions with us has realized that this was not the proper time to play politics.
They have also realized that they should provide some leadership. Mr. Speaker, Canadian municipalities have been wiser than the New Democratic Party. The municipal representatives who are as qualified as we are have understood the message. They are aware that this is not the time for politicizing but to resolve the issue. They have decided to join us in the struggle against inflation. Many businessmen and union members understood. Of course, the executives of some unions which you so well represent do not understand because they are afraid. They want to justify their existence. And my hon. colleagues say that it is at the expense of workers. We are taking that step specifically to assist workers because the unemployed were former union members whom unfortunately the unions are now betraying. We are helping those people to make sure that they will re-enter the labour market and they will surely not do so thanks to your co-operation and your example.
This program, Mr. Speaker, does not discriminate amongst Liberal, Conservative or NDP ridings. The program is fair for everyone. All public employees will be subjected to restrictions. Canadians generally believe in such a program because they feel it is quite realistic. If the creation of 25 jobs in the Public Service was announced, you would see many applicants. There is no ... an hon. member is laughing over there. He knows that a large number of Canadians would like to become public servants specifically to enjoy security of employment which cannot be found in the private sector and to receive salaries which are ... 1 am convinced Mr. Speaker that the hon. member is trying to prevent us from making our comments and make me run out of time.

Mr. Speaker, I will probably not use the 40 minutes allocated to the speaker of the party introducing an amendment. It is my pleasure on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) to introduce Motion No. 9 and to speak as briefly as possible on this motion and the debate before us.
All of us realize that our country is in very serious and dire economic straits. We share this dilemma, admittedly, with a number of other countries in the western world. But nowhere in the world, particularly in the western world among the people with whom we trade, is this crisis as deep, as profound and as devastating as is our experience here in Canada.
We say that inflation is the cause of this serious problem. Up to this point it has been a favourite pastime of this government and of other important and powerful players in the economy, like the corporate sector and unions, to say that inflation is crippling our economy, destroying our freedom and destroying our ability to manage the resources of this great country in the manner best suited to our needs. We hear it said, "Let us all now step out and fight inflation". This is what is being preached throughout the land. But we also hear it said, "If 1 am not right there when we get started, just get started without me and don't wait. Somebody make a beginning."
But we have to come to grips with the problem of inflation to restore once again confidence and faith in our country and to give substance, belief and foundation to the great security systems that we have, and to the social contracts that we have planned and put in place for ourselves. As we all know, the government is in a position today where in some instances it is defaulting on social contracts in which it has entered. One example is the removal of indexation, which is part of the last instalment in the federal budget. That was a social contract. Another is the question of collective bargaining, which has caused all of us some difficulty and which has invited the wrath and the anger of our friends in the New Democratic Party.
As we all know, the best security system in the world and the best security system any government could offer is a job and peace of mind, knowing that one's savings will not be ravaged by inflation or a government's economic mismanagement.
Every speaker who has participated in the debate following the budget, particularly those who have participated in this debate, are to blame for the situation that we are in. Members
on all sides are to blame. We sought to attach blame for the incredible situation that we have got ourselves into. Even the government would have to admit that not all of the misery dispensed has been imported from some other part of the world. We have managed to shoot ourselves in the foot quite ably by ourselves. It was not the Americans or any other country that told us we should have a Foreign Investment Review Agency which, at the moment, does nothing else but scare and frighten away the scarce and much needed investment capital. No one in the rest of the world told us that we should have a National Energy Program, which has literally destroyed and probably rendered impotent the most vital sector in our economy today. These wounds are self-inflicted and the misery that results from them is distributed not in a very fair and equitable manner. As we all know, there are some people who actually profit from inflation and there are some people who actually profit from the misery of others.
We hear our friends to the left speak about equity, fairness and the equal distribution of wealth. They always say that, without accepting an equal share of the misery and the hardship and the determination to straighten out the mess. The necessity for that also applies to my friends on the left.
We know who is to blame. It is now believed that the term ministerial responsibility is really a contradiction because we see no examples of ministerial responsibility. Certainly in the last two or three years, none of our ministers of the Crown or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have accepted any blame for anything. They brought in a budget in November. In June they returned and said that they had made a little mistake. They have rendered thousands of small businesses insolvent and have thrown the country into bankruptcy. They said that they had made a little miscalculation; they thought the deficit was to be $10 billion and it turned out to be $20 billion. Now they say they have seen the light and have some new ideas. They ask us to hang on, that they will show us something different.
We all know that if there were any ministerial responsibility left, or if any of them were willing to accept ministerial responsibility, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) would have had to offer his resignation and let someone else try something fresh. This goes as well for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who fought tooth and nail a couple of years ago to bring in the National Energy Program, which was to secure energy self-sufficiency by the year 1990 and to ensure above 50 per cent Canadian ownership content. Now we know that neither of these goals will be achieved. But has the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources resigned? Of course no, because as we all know the term "ministerial responsibility" is not in fact a contradiction in terms.
1 did not want to use the time available to me to attach blame to any one of the players in the economy, because 1 assumed that at least those who are in the chamber this


evening and, indeed, most people who take the time to turn on their television sets to watch our debates know full well who is to blame and where the buck should stop.
1 compare our situation to a ship which has run aground. Luckily there was no loss of life, but the ship is sitting on a sandbank and we are all floating away in lifeboats. When you are in a lifeboat, you do not make judgments or hold court on who is to blame for the predicament. What we do is all get together to try to make the best of the situation. We look at what the options are. Our aim is to stay alive as an important industrial nation in the world and as an equal and respected partner in the community of the western economy. In so doing, we have to make some fundamental commitments to change the way we have behaved as partners in the economy within our country. Again, it is up to the government to take the lead in showing some new direction.
Anyone listening to the debate over the last couple of days would know that it is simply not true that there were no constructive suggestions by the opposition to help the government find its way out of the dilemma. There is no easy and simple solution. This is a fact with which we all agree. But some constructive suggestions have been made in terms of Bill C-124, which was designed to portray the government as finally accepting some responsibility and showing the lead without, in the very initial period, imposing restrictive and comprehensive measures to force everyone into a certain stream.
The government has said that it will restrain itself and its employees to a wage package which will not exceed 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the following year. Of course there are various complications with such an approach. Many of our friends and colleagues have pointed out some of these problems. The misery which a senior civil servant in the $90,000 to $105,000 range will have to suffer with a 6 per cent increase in his salary will of course be much easier to bear than that of a public servant in the $12,000 per year range. Usually both have to buy their groceries in the same supermarket, and yet one will receive a $6,000 increase and the other might receive a $700 increase in one year.
I have looked at the total package and have listened with great care to the defence of the government in support of this so called 6 per cent world. I am still very uneasy because I happen to think that the idea could work, if the government did not limit this restraint to its own public servants and, incidentally, to our own employees. It is grossly unfair that employees of Members of Parliament should have their salaries rolled back. 1 am not entirely convinced the arguments of the New Democratic Party with respect to this bill, which they are vehemently opposing in general, are correct. At the outset they said that regardless of whether we accept or reject their amendments, they are opposed to this kind of approach. 1 happen to think, as is always the case with socialists, that the greatest of all human failings, greed, applies to them more than it does to capitalists. They are really more interested in the 6 per cent reduction of their own salaries than anything else. It would be an exercise in intellectual honesty if they
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
admitted it. 1 personally do not think that Members of Parliament are overly generously rewarded, but I do not think that a system such as the one proposed would work unless we took the lead and showed some restraint. If this restraint were carried throughout the system, I think it would work.
Naturally I am disappointed already because we learned that the government has found ways to protect certain of its friends from the impact of this measure. We are told that regulatory agencies will be given certain guidelines. They can award to Crown corporations or to regulated industries increases in their charges and tariffs in excess of 6 per cent, but any such settlement or benefit to a Crown corporation will have to be reviewed by cabinet. There is no doubt in my mind-and I have watched the government now for ten years-that there will be certain friends who will convince the government that their input costs have been too great; that if they are tied to the 6 per cent rate they will have to reduce services, which will be harmful to its political welfare; and that they should be allowed to make additional charges. We have seen examples of this already.
It will be interesting to see how Bell Canada, other regulated Crown corporations and private agencies will be treated in response to their demands. When 1 say that I support and think the program will work, 1 qualify it by those comments. If we stick to our guns, when we return to our constituencies businessmen will be able to see their telephone rates, hydro bills and natural gas bills, restricted to a 6 per cent increase if the government forgoes further increases in gasoline prices. In other words, if all regulated industries, products and services dispensed throughout the country are restricted to a 6 per cent increase, the program would have an excellent chance of working.
1 cast my mind back to the time when I managed a business. Certainly, if I could have seen the government taking initiatives with conviction and strength, I would have had no problem convincing employees working in my firm that the time had come for all of us to follow the lead because there was a chance we could come to grips with some of the serious problems faced by the nation.
Let me come to the problem of one of the shortcomings in this bill which is the collective bargaining process. As we know, the bill introduced certain restrictions to this process of collective bargaining. Reasonably one could ask, "What is the sense of bargaining if you already know that you are tied to a 6 per cent ceiling?" The ceiling will become the floor and the floor will become the ceiling, so everybody will get a 6 per cent increase. Surely no one is going to bargain for anything less. So what is the sense of bargaining collectively?
If we were convinced this is a program that will work and will legislate this program into place, what was the reason for saying then that you cannot bargain collectively? It follows logically, except of course that there are other things that unions and groups of workers bargain for. We have certain commitments to affirmative action programs, for instance. I


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
have said that the bill is unfair in terms of the great differential in the wage scale where we have senior bureaucrats earning in excess of $100,000 and we have some employees of the federal government who are in the very lowest of pay scales. Therefore there could have been a process of collective bargaining to close this gap and to make some necessary adjustments. There are some legitimate problems that the women's groups have made us aware of and that are involved in this affirmative action program. Maybe there is room for some collective bargaining to overcome and straighten out some of these problems. Unfortunately, the government moved to restrict the process of collective bargaining, and that is terribly unfortunate because certain groups who are crucial to making this program work will, for that reason, opt out.
If you cast your mind to the time in 1974 when my party proposed a program of wage and price controls you will recall that we had intended to introduce a 90-day freeze. When I think back to that particular election campaign, I remember that it was not very difficult for me to get people to join us in that campaign because we were able to make the commitment that for 90 days the price of gasoline, butter, bread and whatever you needed to buy would not increase. There was no need to set up a monitoring agency or police force because if anyone in any supermarket or anywhere else increased their prices it was quite obvious that it would not have taken more than 30 seconds for someone to know that someone else had been breaking the law.
You will also recall that after that 90-day freeze we had proposed an 18-month period of adjustment, and that is precisely the kind of adjustment that we had in mind, because, as we all know if we want to be honest with ourselves, we have established in our society and in our economy certain elites. Those are, first of all, the corporate or the public elite, the government and its friends, the bureaucracy, insensitive, stubborn, with ravenous appetites for our tax dollars, and, as I have already said, accountable to no one. That is a certain elite and I am not including in that elite the lower paid public servants who are performing throughout our country a very useful, vital and essential service to all of us.
Then there is the other elite and that is the corporate elite. That is mainly the control sector of the economy. Those are the people who, again in a monstrous and ravenous way, have gobbled up all the available resources of the country, not to create new jobs, not to create new enterprises, but to use all the money that our banks have available, and even some the government had available that it had taken from other taxpayers, to gobble up existing companies, to enlarge their sphere of influence and to concentrate and to integrate their large corporate entities.
One cannot blame the large corporations for doing that because no one in their right mind would start any new enterprise today at a time when there is such uncertainty about where the government is going and what the future intent of the government will be in becoming involved as an active partner in the economy.
If the National Energy Program and Canagrex are any indication of what the government intends to do in the future, I certainly, if I were free to do so tomorrow, would not start a new business in this country. 1 suppose that a lot of large corporate decision-makers have come to the same conclusion. So what do they do? Instead of expanding their plants, creating new jobs, doing research and development to produce new products and getting out in the world to sell these products, they have simply engaged in an exercise which I call corporate cannibalism by gobbling up other companies and enlarging their sphere of influence in that way.
That has had a devastating effect on the economy, particularly since the banks were willing partners in this scheme of corporate cannibalism. Some banks are in such dire straits today. There is no question about that, because of loans they have handed out to Dome Petroleum and to other major companies which are, for all intents and purposes, insolvent today, that they have to call back loans made to small businessmen who are paying their interest and struggling away, despite the adversity and the difficulties that they are encountering.
We have this corporate elite. It is usually the regulated sector of the economy. The government tells them to what extent they can increase the cost of their services or the products they produce, and the government has them completely regulated in every way. Unfortunately, if we compare our corporate sector with that of the United States, we find that our large corporations have always been very willing to be regulated by government. The reason is that they felt there is a certain amount of security in that, because should they get into trouble the government will give out, offer letters of comfort, loan guarantees or even cash. As long as they are big enough, as long as they employ a lot of people, the government will come to their aid.
And their judgment was right. If you look at Dome Petroleum, no one in their right mind really believes that this government will allow Dome Petroleum to go under. They have been too willing and too helpful in bringing the National Energy Program about, and friends always help each other, so the government will bail out Dome Petroleum. Unfortunately, the government of course will not be able to bail out everybody, so it has to be very selective in the way that these bailouts are being conducted. Some peple who have the ear of certain ministers will, of course, get help and others will be allowed to go under and die.
The third elite is the labour elite. When one looks into the background of this elitism which is in charge of our economy, one finds that the one third of our labour force, numbering approximately 12.2 million, that is unionized, is employed by the corporate elite of which I have spoken. While it is not fair to say this about all organized labour, to a great extent the organized one third component of the labour force that is

u:



unionized works for the corporate elite. The corporate managers no longer understand, and certainly this government has long forgotten, the most basic principles of a free market economy, which is supply and demand, or the invisible hand which regulates the economy. I have said before in the House that the invisible hand has become the invisible handshake. It is the invisible handshake between Dennis McDermott, the CP group of companies and these large corporations whose products are regulated but whose future is protected by the government, the third partner in the elitist conspiracy.
The present situation is that this blue chip elite, made up of corporations, is now in dire straits. These are the same corporations which the government is now calling in to advise it this fall on what it should do in terms of developing better measures to turn the economy around. I shudder to think what the outcome of that dialogue will be. However, these people are now in dire straits. The corporate elite is not producing any revenues for the government, so it is defaulting on its social contract. The corporate elite is in dire straits because it can no longer increase its prices according to what the union demands because the government wants to regulate the end price of their products. This reaction has caused our ship to run aground.
When the system is running smoothly and everyone is able to eat, has a place to live and can afford to go on a vacation once a year, even the low-paid paid worker, then of course no one complains. But the corporate elite and the labour elite are now being asked to take a share of the misery that our present economic circumstances dictate. Therefore they are squealing. The squeals are heard no louder than those of our friends to the left, the New Democratic Party. That party represents no one else in the House but one partner in that group of elite. That is, labour. They are upset because of this attack on collective bargaining.
To conclude, 1 would like to focus on that particular component. I firmly believe that as long as our unions insist, so stubbornly on adhering to this adversary process in which they like to engage, we will not be able to repair the damage that has been done to our economy on a permanent basis. As long as this juvenile and outdated method of collective bargaining in industrial relations continues we will simply be unable to devise and chart a plan of economic recovery.
1 would yet have to meet a union boss who would not much rather sit in the boardroom to help make decisions that would ensure the health and welfare of the company and create new wealth, which could ultimately be passed on to the employees of that company, than sit in the lunchroom and plot how to destroy the company and hinder any effort on the part of the corporate managers to create new wealth. I would yet have to meet a union leader who would not much rather discuss profitsharing, for example. However, if he had to discuss profitsharing with his boss he would also have to accept the responsibility of working together with his boss to create wealth and profit before sharing it.
That is why we call people who never appear to have anything and want to share it with everybody else socialist. You cannot distribute wealth that you have not first created. That
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
is as true for the smallest business as it is for the largest corporation. It is certainly true for the managers who are in charge of looking after the public interest.
1 am not blaming the corporations for our present situation or for their contribution to our present problems. 1 am not saying that the unions are to blame. As I have said, the buck stops at one place only, and that is here, at the treasury benches across the aisle.
If the corporate sector behaves responsibly there is no need to compete with it in the public interest. We should proceed as does every other country, which is to make laws and regulations within which the corporate sector must operate. If free enterprise has been the basis of the prosperity of a nation such as ours, it then must operate within certain principles of the free enterprise system. This means competition. Perhaps we should be considering competition laws, or anti-trust laws as they are called in the United States. When a corporate entity becomes too integrated or monopolistic, or when a group of corporations become too oligopolistic, a government should intervene and force them to divest themselves of certain holdings to assure the maintenance of fair competition.
The blame belongs to the government for its deliberate policy of neglect which allows this kind of situation to occur and for giving the banks the leeway which they have to plan with the corporations in the scheme of corporate cannibalism.
The unions are not to blame for the power which is not due to any group of workers. Under present circumstances, two thirds of the workers are not unionized and do not have an opportunity to be unionized because the large unions are not interested in those who work in the private sector and have to compete in the free market economy. They are the ones who are paying the bills.
I am not blaming the unions, either for the power they have, which is a power, if one can imagine it, to compel every person who works in the federal or provincial public sector to be in the union. Every person who wants a job with the federal or provincial government is compelled to belong to the union. We have a great chartered principle of democracy called freedom of association which was entrenched in our Constitution, in the wisdom of those who supported the entrenchment of certain aspects and principles of democracy. This applies to every Canadian except to members of unions. They have no choice. They either belong or they do not work for the federal or provincial government or the CP group of companies or any other large integrated corporate entities. It would also include any large industry where wages are usually double those in unregulated industries, like the construction industry, teachers, and so on. Those are the people who are compelled to belong to unions.
That is totally inconsistent with one of the most cardinal principles of democracy. When we speak about embarking or setting out on a road of economic recovery, and we look around at the rest of the world, at Japan, Sweden, or Germany, and we ask why it is that some of the problems we are experiencing are not experienced in those parts of the world,


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
we may find that it might well be for reason. For instance, it is said that Sweden is mainly a socialist country and West Germany is certainly a socialist country. Yet that cardinal principle, freedom of association, is respected. In fact, I have statistical comparisons. In the West German labour force, it is precisely one third of the work force which has chosen to belong to unions. But every person who works, any worker in any sector of the economy, has the opportunity to belong to a union, because a union does not obtain certification from any of the provincial governments or the federal government unless it makes itself available for membership to every person who works.
Would your Honour agree with me that that would be a much better system? Would union leaders in this country not be much more responsible if they had to compete for the affection of their members instead of behaving as if they lived in some kind of one-party democracy to which some of the Iron Curtain socialist countries subscribe? Would Your Honour not believe that a fellow like Dennis McDermott would think twice before he stood on the steps of this place and said that, "The next time we meet, we will be meeting inside if these turkeys in there do not behave"? Would Your Honour not believe that a fellow like that would have to think twice before he said that because otherwise he may well see mass resignations?
I happen to think that the workers in the country, at least the people who support me, the people with whom I sit in the lunchroom, the people who have worked for me over the years, have as much at stake in this economy and in the future of this great country and love this country as much as you and I do, and they want to do as much for it as you and I do, and do not want to be irresponsible. They do not want to break the laws of this country deliberately. Certainly, they do not appreciate their leaders doing and saying things which are irresponsible and derisive.
Therefore I say that before the NDP gets up in this House and fights for the survival of the collective bargaining process, a process to which I subscribe wholeheartedly, but under different management and circumstances, its members should seek counsel among themselves and say what it is about this collectivism that they are defending. It is the kind of collectivism which operates in socialist countries behind the Iron Curtain, this kind of one-party collectivism, this one-party democratic process where people can elect someone but the choice is limited to one party.
I would like to conclude with just one sentence. It does not make sense for us to criticize this bill if we are not prepared to take the lead ourselves in setting some goals and objectives which will be reasonable and will signal to the rest of the country that we, ourselves, are serious. We have said that we will reduce our own salaries by 6 per cent. We have said that we will insist that the people who work for us will restrain themselves to a 6 per cent increase. I think that that is a signal, and if we are earnest and serious about it, the rest of the country might follow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after hearing the last anti-union tirade, I am in some ways grateful that I
am able to speak after that rather negative representation made by the representative of the Conservative Party. Since the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) allowed the hon. member who just spoke to speak as his replacement with regard to his amendment, I presume that what the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) stated is the policy of the Conservative Party when it comes to unions in this country. I find that interesting. I only have about 15 minutes in which to speak, if I am also to allow the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) to contribute in the time remaining. I find it interesting that very few of the Liberal or Conservative members from whom we have heard in this debate have really spoken about the effects of this legislation. When it comes to collective bargaining, there is an assumption in the country that the government has moved to allow collective bargaining actually to take place. Let me read from the bill which is before us. Clause 7 states:
The parties to a collective agreement, or the persons bound by an arbitral award, that includes a compensation plan that is extended under section 4 may, by agreement, amend any terms and conditions of the collective agreement or arbitral award other than wage rates or other terms and conditions of the compensation plan.
What that government position means is that not only must the employees want to negotiate, they must also seek leave and permission of their employer before they can even start negotiations. That means that Ian Sinclair's workers at Canadian Pacific must receive his permission before they can open negotiations. That means that the employees of the various Crown corporations must seek the permission of those Crown corporations before they can negotiate. That means that workers who work for the public service, for the people of Canada, will have to receive the permission of the various ministers and of the President of the Treasury Board before they can even open negotiations. That goes against every principle of negotiating under the laws of this land, against the right to negotiate, not only one's salary but the other terms and conditions of one's work. That is a right which cannot be arbitrarily denied by one's employer, be it government, Crown corporation or private sector company.
We should consider the Conservative amendment because they have spoken as though they had some new solutions, as though they had a different approach to the whole debate. Amendment No. 9 states:
Subject to subsection (2), parties to a collective agreement, or the persons bound by an arbitral award, that includes a compensation plan that is extended under section 4 may, by agreement, amend any terms and conditions-
That is, with the exception of money. Again, the Conservative Party members, who parade in this House as the people who are fighting to bring back collective bargaining rights, are admitting by their own amendment that collective bargaining will only occur with the gracious permission of the employer. So let us not have any more hypocrisy in this House. Let us have the truth from the Conservative Party. The Tories will vote for the bill, but their amendment will not restore collective bargaining. Their amendment will not even guarantee that workers will have the right to open negotiations.


Let us presume that the negotiation procedure has been opened, that negotiations on non-monetary items have proceeded, and that there is still some sort of dispute or deadlock. What would happen under the provisions of this bill? Under the provisions of the bill as it now stands, nothing would happen. If the workers and the employers disagree, there would be no solution to the impasse.
In committee, the President of the Treasury Board said that perhaps they could agree to voluntary arbitration. It is very unlikely that employers will agree to voluntary arbitration on items they cannot negotiate with their employees. They had just gone through a process of negotiation. They have not come to any resolution of the disputes they have. Now, according to the President of the Treasury Board, they may try voluntary arbitration. Obviously that is not a solution.
What does the Conservative amendment say? It says that these measures could go to binding arbitration, as long as there is no talk about money. They deny the right to strike, which is guaranteed to many workers under the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the Canada Labour Code. In other words, they are against legislation presently existing on the books of this country.
They also say by their amendment that maternity leave, pensions and other items that are negotiated must come under the 6 per cent. That is the position in the amendment they put forward.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) stated in the House last Friday that negotiating within the 6 per cent is a good idea. It allows for maternity leave, for pensions and for workers at the top of the scale to get 2 per cent and for those at the bottom to get 9 per cent. That in principle sounds wonderful to the Conservative Party. They fail to recognize that within most collective bargaining agreements, the range is not that wide. You are talking about somebody earning $20,000 receiving a 2 per cent increase and somebody earning $10,000 receiving a 9 per cent increase.
That is the reality of what the Conservative Party is saying. It sounds great. You get the impression from the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands that somebody earning $80,000 or $90,000 would settle for a 2 per cent increase in order to help someone earning $10,000. In reality, with most collective bargaining agreements the spread is not that much and they tend to be lumped together. The low-paid tend to be lumped within one collective agreement and the high-paid within another. Therefore, the 6 per cent solution is no solution at all.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) said, the people who will suffer tend to be in the bargaining unions which basically represent women workers, those with low salaries. They are the bargaining units that tend to represent those in the cleaning or clerical jobs, those who, according to the Public Service Commission annual report of 1981, earn between $10,000 and $15,000. Thirteen per cent of the government workers fall in that range and 29.3 per cent fall in the range between $15,000 and $20,000.
In that 43 per cent range you find most of the poorly paid workers, most of whom are women. How are they going to
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
resolve the problems they face with the Conservative and Liberal 6 per cent solution?
It is interesting at last to see the minister responsible for the Status of Women in the chamber. It is unfortunate that she has not said one word in this debate. It is unfortunate that the Liberal members on the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee who studied this bill clause by clause would not allow the minister responsible for the status of women to appear in person, regardless of what her position is on this legislation.

Yes, I will sit down in five minutes. I challenge the minister to get up in this House and state her position on this bill. Our position is that the laws passed by Parliament, the Canada Labour Code and the Public Service Staff Relations Act should be used to complete each and every set of negotiations. The government may have some guidelines of 6 per cent and 5 per cent or it may change that guideline to 10 per cent and 9 per cent, depending on what happens to the cost of living. However, the regular laws of this land which allow unions and companies to open negotiations and negotiate in order to come to some dispute-resolving method if negotiations break down are the procedures which should be followed in his country.
I wish to quote from a letter from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) to The Globe and Mail. It is very nice to see him in the Chamber. His letter reads in part:
The right to strike is one of the important cornerstones of a free and democratic society ... There is clearly room for greater co-operation between unions and employers, and Parliament has entrusted to Labour Canada the responsibility for assisting in the development and maintenance of constructive relationships.
Parliament has entrusted that responsibility to Labour Canada. Where was the Minister of Labour when this bill was being debated? He did not speak once in the last month during this debate. Nor did he appear before the committee. That same Liberal majority refused to allow that minister to appear, if he had the courage to do so. We will never know because the Liberal majority prevented that. It is interesting to see his remarks on the right to strike, it being an important cornerstone in a free and democratic society. It is important to note that this bill denies and takes away the right of those groups within the Crown corporations and, in some cases, government workers.
Collective bargaining has not been restored. The Conservative Party does not wish to restore it. The Liberal government will make sure it is not restored. The Minister of Labour will remain silent.
Our Amendment No. 11 in my name and the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East guarantees that maternity leave can be negotiated and also guarantees that it will not be considered part of the 6 per cent and 5 per cent. In our amendments Nos. 2 and 11 we exclude maternity leave from the


Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
definition of compensation and from the 6 per cent ceiling that this government wishes to impose.
It is our belief that this basic human right, which speaks to the very heart of equality and is of concern to so many families, cannot be ignored by this Parliament. I challenge all members, whether Conservative or Liberal, to get up in this House and support an amendment which guarantees that maternity leave can be negotiated and that it will not come from the pockets of the very poorly paid workers within that bargaining unit.
We have suggested similar treatment for pensions in Motion No. 2 and in Motion No. 14. We have said that pensions must be excluded from the definition. We have said that workers in their last two years of work will make sacrifices in addition to limiting increases in their wages to 6 per cent and 5 per cent for the next two years. They will be making sacrifices each and every day of their lives, and so will their families. Their spouses will be sacrificing each and every day of their lives. Most pensions which are adequate-and they are not for the most part in the country-are based on the last five years' income. By restricting the incomes of workers in the last two years of their employment we are restricting their incomes for the rest of their lives. In addition to that, the 6 per cent and 5 per cent provisions of this bill will exclude the right of unions to negotiate to strengthen weak pension plans. These are reasonable amendments made with restraint in mind with the recognition that there is some need for government leadership on this issue, but this bill does not provide that leadership. It does not even come close to providing it.
I recognize my time is limited. I would like to say one more thing before sitting down. I remind the Conservative members of what their leader said in an interview published last Thursday. I remind them of this because they will be voting in I 5 minutes. Their leader said:
1 would reject controls. And I wouldn't allow my PMO to be issuing rumours that they were coming in while I was saying that they weren't. I think that controls won't work.
I agree with the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), and I will be very interested to see how he and his colleagues will vote in 15 minutes.
