speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few minutes in which to raise a few points in response to the comments of the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). I would also like to leave a few minutes-unfortunately, they will be very few-to my friend, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), who has indicated some interest in making some comments before the debate closes this evening.
Much has been made by my friend, the hon. member for Churchill, of the fact that Bill C-124 would restrict collective bargaining. We agree that it would indeed restrict collective bargaining, and we tried in the course of the committee hearings-I would like at this point to thank the members who participated in those hearings for their very constructive
contributions-to open up the collective bargaining process through the amendment to Clause 7. This now permits parties to negotiate non-monetary items-the one which immediately springs to mind is the issue of health and safety-during the course of a collective agreement.
I suggest that the hon. member for Churchill and his colleagues have tended to discount the significance of that provision. 1 suggest to hon. members that it indeed restores one of the most important aspects of collective bargaining and preserves collective bargaining during the period when the program envisaged by the bill is in effect.
We have heard much exaggeration. I cannot help but go back for a moment to the principles of the ILO to which I referred the other day. Those principles are found at page 19873 of Hansard for July 30. The following statement is made in the ILO Geneva-77 principles at page 15:
-the (ILO) supervisory bodies have not ignored the serious problems that may arise in certain circumstances in the economic field, and they have accordingly stated that it would be difficult to lay down an absolute rule concerning voluntary collective bargaining because, under certain circumstances, governments might feel that the economic position of their countries called at certain times for stabilization measures during the application of which it would not be possible for wage rates to be fixed freely through the medium of collective bargaining. Nevertheless, any such restriction should be imposed as an exceptional measure and only to the extent that is necessary, without exceeding a reasonable period, and it should be accompanied by adequate safeguards to protect workers' living standards.
I cite that again because clearly the program of wage restraint introduced by the government in Bill C-124 is indeed on all fours with the criteria set forward in that statement from the ILO.
Let me turn for a moment to the specific amendment which stands in the name of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). It is argued that that amendment would do more than what we have proposed in terms of providing for a degree of collective bargaining during the period of this program. In fact, if one looks carefully at the proposed amendment-and I see the hon. member for Rosedale in the House-one will see that in many important respects the amendment is more stringent and places more of a strait-jacket on the parties than what we have proposed in our amendment, which also stands on the Order Paper. Specifically, the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Rosedale suggests a total compensation approach within the limits of 6 per cent and 5 per cent. Our own amendment is very flexible in that it does not propose such criteria. I have stated that it is the government's intention that when parties-employers and employees-are able to reach an agreement within the over-all criteria of 6 per cent and 5 per cent, they can be released from the application of the law or the law can be terminated with respect to that particular group by order in council. In the case of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Rosedale there is a strict adherence of total compensation to the six and five approach. 1 suggest this means that any incremental adjustments which would otherwise be available, particularly to those groups at the lower end of the pay scale, would have to be included, under the terms of this proposal, in the 6 per cent and 5 per


cent, and therefore this would make it impossible to provide some of these groups with compensation to which they would otherwise be entitled in accordance with the government's proposal.
Specifically, I refer to the example of clerks which was raised in committee. It is clear that in the case of clerks in certain instances there will be incremental payments moving clerks toward job rates which could be as much as 3 per cent, thereby in certain cases, at the lower end of the scale, providing for compensation increases in a given year of as much as 9 per cent. It was specifically to prevent incremental steps taking place at the higher end of the scale that an amendment was introduced by the government in committee which is found in Clause 6(5) where it states:
Employees or groups of employees whose salary range as of June 29,1982 has a maximum that equals or exceeds forty-nine thousand five hundred dollars shall not-
For the period of the program.
-be entitled to the merit increases or performance awards that would, but for this subsection, form part of their compensation plan.
This includes incremental increases. Under the proposal of the hon. member for Rosedale lower paid groups, those who earn less than $49,500-I think of clerks in particular, who have often been cited by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald)-would not be entitled to receive incremental increases except within the 6 per cent and 5 per cent total compensation package which, I suggest, is much more stringent than our proposed approach under the amendment which has been tabled by the government. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Rosedale is considerably less fair to lower paid groups.
I presume it is for one of these reasons that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands lauded the amendment which was tabled by the government last Thursday night. I referred earlier to her comments as reported in last Friday's Citizen where she said that the announcement goes a long way toward quelling Tory opposition to the bill. She said that the federal government had done a complete somersault on the bill during the past few days and that the amendment should help workers at the lower end of the wage scale. She said, "I think it will give much more equity within the six and five limit."
I was struck and pleased by the objectivity of her comments, notwithstanding the fact that there was also a Tory announcement which was also directed toward opening up the collective bargaining process.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the intent of our amendment, to permit groups to strike their own deal, reach their arrangements within the six and Five limit and then be released from the application of the law through an order of the governor in council, is much more appropriate, much more flexible and much more equitable and also preserves in total collective bargaining within the six and five limit.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
It is true that the Tory amendment also suggests that there should be a system of arbitration making reference to the Canada Labour Code in the proposed amendment and specifically, as I recall, to certain sections, namely Sections 155 to 159 of the code which are for the adjudication of dispute purposes and not for the arbitration of interest purposes, and use those sections to settle disputes between the parties.
I suggest that arbitral awards during the period of this program would very likely establish precedents which would be unacceptable and which would not have taken place in the normal course of collective bargaining. These awards would undoubtedly prove more expensive in the longer term. We saw an arbitral award earlier this week in the Province of Ontario, which greatly extended maternity leave benefits, for example, during this period of restraint. Our purpose is to restrain costs, not increase costs, and I suggest that arbitral awards could increase costs during the duration of this program.
Nor only that, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that many parties would object to the imposition of compulsory arbitration during this period, where we have provided a means of sound, firm and fair collective bargaining.
I would also remind hon. members that with respect to binding arbitration under the Canada Labour Code, 1 am advised that there is no appeal to a higher authority. Therefore, I submit that any form of arbitration-and I have much more to say on this subject-would be most inappropriate.
I must leave at least a moment to my friend, the hon. member for Capilano, to make at least some comments. I regret that the clock does not permit me to offer him more time for his comments.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) for the courtesy of allowing me a minute to offer a few remarks. I wish him well with the voluntary restraint program which he is appealing to the country to accept in Bill C-124.
When he talks about the arbitration aspect of this bill I have to wonder why he has not given the House of Commons and its staff the opportunity for arbitration through the Commissioners of Internal Economy. Instead of having Treasury Board reach its arms and tentacles into the management of the affairs of the House of Commons, surely the arbitration of pay for the staff that serves individual members of the House should come under the Commissioners of Internal Economy and not under Treasury Board. It is most unnatural and unjust that Treasury Board should roll back awards that have already been granted to the staff that serves members of the House of Commons.
It is most unfair that Treasury Board would take this action against a small group of unorganized employees who serve us without tenure, work long hours into the night and sometimes early in the morning-this unorganized group is saving the government about $480,000 per year through this Treasury Board action. The government wastes more than 200 times that amount on advocacy advertising.
